quiz.explanation: **2...c6**: now it's 1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5, your Caro-Kann.

d5-gambits.title: Gambits and offbeat 1.d4: Blackmar-Diemer, Veresov, 2.Bg5, Grob
extra_anchors: 1. d4 d5 2. e4 dxe4 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. f3 exf3 5. Nxf3 e6
1. d4 d5 2. Nc3 Nf6 3. Bg5
d5-gambits.summary: Gambits work at club level because people panic. Your rule: **take the pawn when it's safe, then build the usual house (...e6, ...Be7, ...O-O, ...c5) and give the pawn back only for development.** Against early bishop moves (2.Bg5, Veresov), ask the bishop with ...h6 and hit b2.

goals.white: Fast development, open lines (the f-file in the Blackmar-Diemer), and a quick attack on your king.
goals.black: Keep the extra pawn or return it at the right moment, castle, and open the centre with ...c5.

structure.name: Open centre after ...dxe4 (BDG); Veresov/2.Bg5 = QGD-like
structure.description: In the BDG White gives the e- and f-pawns' worth of centre for development; Black has a 4-vs-3 centre and an extra pawn. In the Veresov and 2.Bg5, the structure is a normal ...d5/...e6 one.

pieces.why: Defends h7 and d5; it's the key defender against BDG attacks.
Breaks Bg5 pins.
...Qb6 hits b2 when White's dark bishop has left c1.

key_squares.why: In the BDG d4 is White's weak pawn: hit it with ...c5 and ...Nc6.
White's target on the half-open f-file. Castle quickly.
After an early Bg5/Bf4, b2 is loose.

white.why: Attack along the f-file and against f7.
Rarely, to open lines.

black.why: Hits the d4-pawn; opens the centre while White's king is still not safe.
Against 3.f3 in the BDG: a counter-punch.

plans.title: Blackmar-Diemer: the Euwe Defence
steps: 2...dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3 exf3 5.Nxf3 e6.
You are a pawn up with a safe king.

plans.title: Early bishop moves: ...h6 and ...Qb6
steps: 2.Bg5 h6 3.Bh4 c6 and ...Qb6.

plans.title: Grob 1.g4: protect d5 and take the centre
steps: ...e5 next; White's g-pawn is a weakness.

opponent_plans.title: BDG attack on f7
steps: Bc4, O-O, Ne5, Rf1-f3/Qe1-h4.
Answer: castle, ...c5, and trade the attacking knight.

traps.title: Ryder Gambit: 5.Qxf3? Qxd4
traps.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. e4 dxe4 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. f3 exf3 5. Qxf3 Qxd4
traps.explanation: If White takes back on f3 with the queen, take a second pawn on d4. Black is two pawns up and the engine shows about -1.7.

traps.title: BDG with 3.f3: ...e5!
traps.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. e4 dxe4 3. f3 e5 4. dxe5 Qxd1+ 5. Kxd1 Nc6
traps.explanation: If White plays f3 before Nc3, counter-hit with ...e5. After the queen trade White's king is stuck in the middle and Black develops fast (engine about -1.1).

if_deviates.why: Develop and keep the e4-pawn. Black is better.
Hit d4 before White's attack gets going.
Don't take on e4 twice; develop and play ...e5 or ...c5.
Trade on e4: after 5.Nxe4 dxe4 White struggles to win the e4-pawn back cleanly and Black is a little better.
Now it is a London where ...h6 is a free extra move. Same plan: ...c5, ...Nc6, ...Nf6, ...e6.
Big centre; White's kingside is weak.

mistakes_to_avoid: Grabbing more pawns while your king is uncastled.
In the BDG, trying to hold on to everything: give back a pawn for development if needed.
In the Veresov, playing ...e6 too early: 4.e4 then gives White a French-type position you don't play.
Against 2.Bg5, letting White play e3, Nf3 and Bd3 comfortably. Ask the bishop and hit b2 first.

quiz.question: Blackmar-Diemer. Black to move: which setup is simplest?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. e4 dxe4 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. f3 exf3 5. Nxf3
quiz.explanation: **5...e6** gives you a solid QGD-style setup a pawn up.

quiz.question: White played 5.Qxf3. What do you play?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. e4 dxe4 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. f3 exf3 5. Qxf3
quiz.explanation: **...Qxd4**: the d-pawn is undefended. Black is two pawns up.

quiz.question: 1.d4 d5 2.Bg5. Black to move: what's the plan?
quiz.explanation: Ask the bishop with **...h6**, then hit b2 with ...c6 and ...Qb6: White's dark bishop has left the queenside.

quiz.question: Grob: 1.g4 d5 2.Bg2. Simplest move?
quiz.explanation: **...c6** protects d5 and Black is already much better. ...Bxg4 is also good but invites tactics on b7.

d5-london.title: London System (and Jobava London): ...c5, ...Nc6, ...e6, ...Bd6
d5-london.anchor: 1. d4 d5 2. Bf4 Nf6 3. e3 c5 4. c3 Nc6 5. Nd2 e6 6. Ngf3 Bd6
extra_anchors: 1. d4 d5 2. Bf4 Nf6 3. Nc3
1. d4 d5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Bf4 c5 4. e3 Nc6 5. Nbd2 e6 6. c3 Bd6
d5-london.summary: White builds a pyramid (c3-d4-e3) with the bishop outside on f4. **Hit d4 with ...c5, develop ...Nc6 and ...e6, and offer to trade the London bishop with ...Bd6.** If White trades on d6, ...e5 frees your game. Your old 2...Nc6 scored 46.7% here; this setup is the main line used by strong players.

goals.white: Keep the solid pyramid, play Bd3, Ne5 and f4, and attack your king.
goals.black: Pressure d4, trade White's best piece (the f4/g3-bishop), and get ...e5 or queenside play with ...b6/...Bb7.

structure.name: London pyramid vs QGD wall
structure.description: White's pawns c3-d4-e3 are solid but passive. Black's d5-e6 wall plus ...c5 puts pressure on d4. The key fight is over e5: if White's knight sits there with f4 support, White attacks; if Black trades it or gets ...e5 in, Black is comfortable.

pieces.why: Challenges the London bishop. If Bxd6 Qxd6, the queen controls e5.
Hits d4 and e5. Against Ne5 + f4 it re-routes via e7 to g6 or f5.
After ...b6 it fights for e4 and the long diagonal.
c7/e7 support ...e5; b6 hits b2 when White's bishop has left the queenside.

key_squares.why: The battle square. White's knight wants it; your ...e5 break needs it.
...Ne4 can jump in when White's knight leaves f3.
With the bishop on f4, b2 is unguarded: ...Qb6 ideas.

white.why: The 'London attack': Qf3/Qh5 and Rf3-h3 against your king.
Rare; frees White's game if allowed.
Gives up the centre to get e4 in.

black.why: The main break, played at once.
After Bxd6 Qxd6, or after ...Qc7/...Qe7 and ...Re8.
Sometimes gains queenside space and kicks the Bd3; then ...b5-b4.

plans.title: Bxd6 Qxd6 and ...e5
steps: After 7.Bxd6 Qxd6, castle.
Play ...e5: the London bishop is gone, so nobody controls e5.
Free c8-bishop, equal game.

plans.title: Bishop to g3: ...b6, ...Bb7, re-route the c6-knight
steps: Castle, then ...b6 and ...Bb7.
If Ne5 and f4: ...Ne7-g6 or -f5 to trade or chase the knight.
Do not play ...Bxg3 early (hxg3 helps White's rook).

plans.title: Jobava London (Nc3 + Bf4): ...e6 and ...Bb4 or ...Na6
steps: 4.Nb5 Na6 covers c7; then ...Be7, ...O-O, ...c6 and ...c5.
4.e3 Bb4 pins the knight; then ...c5. If Bd3 and Nge2, ...c4 traps the bishop.

opponent_plans.title: London attack: Ne5, f4, Qf3, Rf3-h3
steps: White masses pieces against h7.
Answer: trade the e5-knight, keep a knight on f6, and open the centre with ...cxd4 or ...c4/...b5.

opponent_plans.title: Qb3 against b7
steps: White hits b7 and d5 when your bishop leaves c8.
Answer: ...Qb6 or ...Qc7; trades of queens are fine for Black.

traps.title: Jobava trap: ...c4 wins the Bd3
traps.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. Bf4 Nf6 3. Nc3 e6 4. e3 Bb4 5. Bd3 c5 6. Nge2 c4
traps.explanation: The d3-bishop has no square: e2 is blocked by the knight, c2 by the pawn, and e4/f5 are covered. Black wins a piece (engine about -5).

traps.title: Bxh7+ doesn't always work
traps.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. Bf4 Nf6 3. e3 c5 4. c3 Nc6 5. Nd2 e6 6. Ngf3 Bd6 7. Bg3 O-O 8. Bd3 b6 9. Ne5 Bb7 10. f4 Ne7 11. Bxh7+ Nxh7
traps.explanation: Don't panic about the Greek gift. Here White has no Ng5 (the knight is on e5) and no fast Qh5, so 11.Bxh7+? just loses a piece (engine about -6.9).

if_deviates.why: Then ...e6 and ...Bd6. Same position after c3 and Nbd2.
Open the c-file and stop Nb5. Then ...Nc6 and ...Bg4 or ...Bf5.
Then ...Bxc5. Black is fully developed; don't try to keep c5.
Trade the bishops, then ...Nc6 and ...e6.
4.Nb5 Na6; 4.e3 Bb4.

mistakes_to_avoid: 2...Nc6 (your old move): blocks the c-pawn, so you never get ...c5.
9...Bxe5? after Ne5: dxe5 kicks your f6-knight and gives White a wedge on e5 (engine +0.8).
...Bxg3 too early: hxg3 opens the h-file for White.
Leaving b7 and d5 loose when White's queen comes to b3.

quiz.question: Black to move. What's the most useful move here?
quiz.explanation: **...c5** hits d4 at once. The London bishop has left b2 and d4 slightly weaker.

quiz.question: White traded on d6. What is Black's freeing move after castling?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. Bf4 Nf6 3. e3 c5 4. c3 Nc6 5. Nd2 e6 6. Ngf3 Bd6 7. Bxd6 Qxd6 8. Bd3 O-O 9. O-O
quiz.explanation: **...e5**: the London bishop is gone, so e5 is yours. Black equalises comfortably.

quiz.question: White has Ne5 and f4. Where should your c6-knight go?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. Bf4 Nf6 3. e3 c5 4. c3 Nc6 5. Nd2 e6 6. Ngf3 Bd6 7. Bg3 O-O 8. Bd3 b6 9. Ne5 Bb7 10. f4
choices: e7, heading for g6 or f5
quiz.explanation: **...Ne7** brings the knight to defend the king and challenge e5 (as in Sandipan-Kryvoruchko).

quiz.question: Jobava London. Black to move after 4.Nb5: what is the simplest defence of c7?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. Bf4 Nf6 3. Nc3 e6 4. Nb5
quiz.explanation: **...Na6** covers c7 for good; later ...c6 kicks the knight back.

quiz.question: Find the reason 6...c4 is strong.
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. Bf4 Nf6 3. Nc3 e6 4. e3 Bb4 5. Bd3 c5 6. Nge2
quiz.explanation: The bishop has no retreat: e2 is blocked by the knight and c2 by the pawn.

sources: Sielecki, Keep It Simple 1.d4 (London chapters, from White's side)

d5-qgd-exchange.title: QGD Exchange: the Carlsbad structure
d5-qgd-exchange.anchor: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. cxd5 exd5
extra_anchors: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. cxd5 exd5 5. Bg5 Be7 6. e3 O-O 7. Bd3 Nbd7 8. Qc2 Re8 9. Nf3 Nf8 10. O-O c6
1. c4 e6 2. Nc3 d5 3. cxd5 exd5 4. d4 Nf6
d5-qgd-exchange.summary: White trades on d5 to fix the pawns. **White attacks on the queenside (b4-b5, the minority attack); Black plays on the kingside and in the centre with ...Ne4, ...f5, ...Ng6.** Your c8-bishop is free now, so the QGD's usual problem is gone.

goals.white: Minority attack: b4-b5 and bxc6 to leave Black a weak pawn on c6 or d5. Or the central plan: Nge2, f3 and e4.
goals.black: Put a knight on e4, re-route the other knight via f8 to g6 or e6, and attack on the kingside before White's queenside play bites.

structure.name: Carlsbad: Black d5+c6 vs White d4+e3, half-open files
structure.description: White has the half-open c-file and a 2-vs-3 pawn majority idea on the queenside (minority attack). Black has the half-open e-file and the e4 outpost. Neither side has a weak pawn yet; whoever's plan runs faster wins.

pieces.why: The dream outpost. It trades White's dark bishop or c3-knight and supports ...f5.
From f8 it guards h7 against Bd3/Qc2; from g6 it eyes h4, f4 and e5.
Uses the half-open e-file, supports ...Ne4.
Now free. Trade it for White's Bd3 (the attacker), or use ...Bg4 against the f3-knight.
Aims at h2. Often comes to d6 after the e7-bishop is traded or re-routed.

key_squares.why: Black's outpost. If White plays f3 to stop it, the e3-pawn becomes weak.
The target of the minority attack. Keep it defended or answer b5 with ...c5 or ...cxb5.
White's knight likes e5; trade it or chase it with ...f6.

white.why: The minority attack: create a weak c-pawn.
Central plan after f3 or Nd2: removes the d5-pawn's support.

black.why: Supports the e4-knight and starts the kingside play (Timman-Short 1988).
Rare but possible when White's pieces leave d4; gives Black hanging pawns.
Slows the minority attack when needed.

plans.title: Knight to e4, then ...f5
steps: ...Ne4 to trade a minor piece.
If White plays Bxe4 dxe4, support e4 with ...f5.
Then ...Be6/...Rad8 and push on the kingside.

plans.title: Knight route f8-g6 and kingside attack
steps: ...h5-h4 or ...Nh4 against g2 (Karpov-Beliavsky 1986).

plans.title: Neutralise the minority attack
steps: Keep ...c6 so bxc6 can be met by ...bxc6 with a protected pawn.
Answer b5 with ...c5 or ...cxb5 when tactics allow.
Trades help Black: fewer pieces to attack c6.

opponent_plans.title: Minority attack
steps: Rab1, b4, a4, b5.
bxc6 bxc6 leaves Black a backward c6-pawn on an open file.

opponent_plans.title: Central break e4
steps: Nge2, f3, then e4.
Opens the centre while Black's pieces are on the kingside.

traps.title: Hold e4 with ...f5, not ...Be6
traps.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. cxd5 exd5 5. Bg5 Be7 6. e3 O-O 7. Bd3 Nbd7 8. Qc2 Re8 9. Nf3 Nf8 10. O-O c6 11. Rab1 Ne4 12. Bxe7 Qxe7 13. Bxe4 dxe4 14. Nd2 Be6 15. Qxe4
traps.explanation: After White wins your knight for his bishop on e4, the new e4-pawn is attacked three times. 14...f5! defends it (equal). 14...Be6? simply drops it to 15.Qxe4.

if_deviates.why: Same structure. Trade White's dark bishop with ...Bd6 and develop the c8-bishop outside.
Same plans; the order doesn't matter in a fixed structure.
White aims for e4. Hit back in the centre before e4 lands.

mistakes_to_avoid: Leaving the d7-knight at home: the f8-g6 route is the heart of Black's play.
Rushing ...Bf5 before castling: Qb3 hits b7 and d5 at the same time.
Answering b5 automatically with ...cxb5 when it leaves d5 weak: think about ...c5 or keeping the tension.
Forgetting h7: while the Bd3/Qc2 battery stares at h7, keep a knight on f6 or f8.

quiz.question: White just played Rab1, preparing b4-b5. What is Black's best plan?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. cxd5 exd5 5. Bg5 Be7 6. e3 O-O 7. Bd3 Nbd7 8. Qc2 Re8 9. Nf3 Nf8 10. O-O c6 11. Rab1
choices: ...Ne4: trade pieces and start kingside play
quiz.explanation: **...Ne4** uses Black's outpost. White's minority attack is slow; Black's kingside play with ...f5 and ...Ng6 is faster.

quiz.question: Which pawn is White's target in the minority attack?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. cxd5 exd5 5. Bg5 Be7 6. e3 O-O 7. Bd3 Nbd7 8. Qc2 Re8 9. Nf3 Nf8 10. O-O c6
quiz.explanation: b4-b5xc6 leaves Black a backward c-pawn on the open c-file.

quiz.question: Black to move. White's bishop took on e4. How do you hold the e4-pawn?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. cxd5 exd5 5. Bg5 Be7 6. e3 O-O 7. Bd3 Nbd7 8. Qc2 Re8 9. Nf3 Nf8 10. O-O c6 11. Rab1 Ne4 12. Bxe7 Qxe7 13. Bxe4 dxe4 14. Nd2
quiz.explanation: **...f5** guards e4 with a pawn and starts the kingside play, as in Timman-Short 1988.

quiz.question: Where does the d7-knight go in the Carlsbad?
quiz.explanation: From f8 it defends h7; from g6 it joins a kingside attack.

sources: Flores Rios, Chess Structures: Carlsbad chapter

d5-qgd-main.title: Queen's Gambit Declined: the Lasker plan vs 4.Bg5, and ...c5 vs 4.Nf3/e3
d5-qgd-main.anchor: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Bg5 Be7 5. e3 O-O 6. Nf3 h6 7. Bh4 Ne4
extra_anchors: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Nf3 Be7 5. Bf4 O-O 6. e3 c5
1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. e3 Be7 5. Nf3 O-O 6. Bd3 dxc4 7. Bxc4 c5
d5-qgd-main.summary: The QGD is cramped but rock-solid. Black's two cures for the cramp: **trade pieces with ...Ne4** (Lasker), and **free the position with ...c5 or ...e5**. Against Bf4 or e3 lines, play ...c5 at once.

goals.white: Use the space edge: pressure on d5 and the c-file, and a kingside attack with Bd3 and Qc2.
goals.black: Trade a pair or two of minor pieces, then break with ...c5 (or ...e5) and develop the c8-bishop.

structure.name: QGD: d5 + e6 against c4 + d4
structure.description: White has more space. Black's e6 pawn shuts in the c8-bishop. After trades on d5 (cxd5 exd5) the bishop is free; after ...dxc4 Black gets ...c5 or ...e5.

pieces.why: In the Lasker it jumps to e4 to trade the c3-knight and force Bxe7.
After Bxe7 Qxe7 she guards the kingside and supports ...e5.
The problem piece. Plan its future early.
Supports ...c5/...e5, then returns to f6 to guard the king.

key_squares.why: Outpost for the knight; trading from e4 relieves the cramp.
The break square. ...c5 hits d4.
Second break square, often after ...dxc4 and ...Nd7.

white.why: Fixes the structure; often leads to Carlsbad (see the Exchange card).
If White gets e4 for free, Black is squeezed. Keep pressure on e4.

black.why: Main freeing break: hits d4, opens the c-file and the b7-bishop's diagonal.
After ...dxc4 and ...Nd7, ...e5 frees the c8-bishop.
Take on c4 only when White's f1-bishop has already moved, so it loses a tempo.

plans.title: Lasker: trade, then break
steps: ...h6 and ...Ne4: force Bxe7 Qxe7.
Trade knights on c3.
Break with ...c5 (Anand vs Topalov 2010) or ...e5.

plans.title: Against 5.Bf4: ...c5 at once
steps: Castle, then ...c5.
After dxc5 Bxc5, develop ...Nc6 and ...Qa5 pinning the c3-knight.
Later ...dxc4 or ...Rd8 against the d-file.

plans.title: Against quiet 4.e3: ...dxc4 and ...c5
steps: Wait for Bd3, then ...dxc4 so the bishop loses a tempo.
If White gets an isolated d4-pawn, blockade on d5.

opponent_plans.title: Squeeze with Rc1, Qc2 and the c-file
steps: White doubles on the c-file against c7/c6.
Answer: trade pieces and play ...c5 to remove the target.

opponent_plans.title: Kingside attack: Bd3, Qc2, Ne5
steps: White hits h7.
Answer: ...h6 early; keep a knight that can return to f6.

traps.title: Recapture first! 8...Nxc3?? loses
traps.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Bg5 Be7 5. e3 O-O 6. Nf3 h6 7. Bh4 Ne4 8. Bxe7 Nxc3 9. Bxd8 Nxd1 10. Be7
traps.explanation: After 8.Bxe7 you must play 8...Qxe7. The 'clever' 8...Nxc3? runs into 9.Bxd8 Nxd1 10.Be7!, saving the bishop with an attack on the rook. White comes out a piece up (engine: about +2.4).

traps.title: 8.Nxe4 Bxh4 9.Nxh4?? dxe4
traps.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Bg5 Be7 5. e3 O-O 6. Nf3 h6 7. Bh4 Ne4 8. Nxe4 Bxh4 9. Nxh4 dxe4
traps.explanation: If White trades on e4 and takes back on h4 with the knight, 9...dxe4 leaves that knight loose: your queen hits it along d8-h4, and the e4-pawn takes away f3. White must play g3, and ...e5 next gives Black the better game (engine about -0.9). White does better with 9.Nc3, keeping the balance.

if_deviates.why: The Exchange Variation: see the Carlsbad card.
Then 5.Bg5 O-O 6.e3 h6 7.Bh4 Ne4 is the same Lasker; 5.Bf4 O-O 6.e3 c5.
When White plays Bd3, take ...dxc4 and play ...c5.
Same as the 5.Bf4 line.
Take the pawn, then ...a6, ...b5, ...Bb7 to fight the g2-bishop.
Same idea: trade, ...c6/...dxc4, ...Nd7 and ...e5 or ...c5.

mistakes_to_avoid: Playing ...dxc4 while White's f1-bishop is still at home and you get nothing for it in development: time it when the bishop has moved.
8...Nxc3?? instead of 8...Qxe7 (see trap).
Forgetting the c8-bishop: without ...b6/...Bb7 or ...e5 it stays a spectator all game.
Lunging with ...g5 to break the pin: it wrecks your kingside. Use ...Be7 and ...Ne4 instead.

quiz.question: Black to move. What is the Lasker idea here?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Bg5 Be7 5. e3 O-O 6. Nf3 h6 7. Bh4
choices: ...Ne4, trading pieces to relieve the cramp
quiz.explanation: **7...Ne4** forces Bxe7 and offers a knight trade. Fewer pieces = less cramp for Black.

quiz.question: White just played 8.Bxe7. What do you play?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Bg5 Be7 5. e3 O-O 6. Nf3 h6 7. Bh4 Ne4 8. Bxe7
quiz.explanation: Recapture. 8...Nxc3? 9.Bxd8 Nxd1 10.Be7! leaves White a piece up.

quiz.question: Black to move. Which break frees Black's game here?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Bg5 Be7 5. e3 O-O 6. Nf3 h6 7. Bh4 Ne4 8. Bxe7 Qxe7 9. Rc1 c6 10. Be2 Nxc3 11. Rxc3 dxc4 12. Bxc4 Nd7 13. O-O b6 14. Bd3
quiz.explanation: **...c5** hits d4 and opens the long diagonal for ...Bb7. Anand did exactly this against Topalov.

quiz.question: White played 5.Bf4 instead of Bg5. Black's plan?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Nf3 Be7 5. Bf4 O-O 6. e3
quiz.explanation: With no pin, **...c5** comes immediately. After dxc5 Bxc5 Black is well developed.

d5-system.title: The ...d5 system: one setup against everything but 1.e4
extra_anchors: 1. Nf3 d5
d5-system.summary: Put a pawn on d5, then build the same house every time: ...Nf6, ...e6, ...Be7 or ...Bd6, ...O-O. Then **break with ...c5** (or ...e5 when White allows it). One structure, one plan, very few tactical holes.

goals.white: Use the extra move to build a strong centre (c4/d4 or a London pyramid) or a kingside attack (Bd3, Ne5, f4).
goals.black: Keep d5 solid, castle quickly, then free the position with ...c5 so your pieces get open lines.

structure.name: QGD wall: pawns on d5 and e6, c-pawn free
structure.description: The pawns on d5 and e6 make an unbreakable wall in the centre. The c-pawn stays on c7 so it can go to c5 and attack d4. That is the difference from your old 2...Nc6, which blocked the c-pawn and left you without a pawn break.

pieces.why: Guards d5 and stops e4. Always the first piece out.
e7 against Bg5 pins (QGD); d6 against the London and Colle, to fight White's dark bishop and aim at h2.
Castle early. Most club losses in these lines come from an uncastled king when the centre opens.
This is the bad piece of the system. Free it with ...b6/...Bb7, or after ...exd5 it gets the c8-h3 diagonal.
c6 after ...c5 (pressure on d4); d7 in the QGD and Carlsbad, heading for f8-g6.

key_squares.why: Your anchor. Never give it up without a reason.
White's dream square. ...Nf6 and ...d5 keep it under control; ...Ne4 is often a great move for you.
Your break square. The ...c5 push attacks d4 and opens the c-file.

white.why: White's main freeing idea in the Colle and London. Stop it, or meet it with ...dxe4 and ...Qc7 pressure.
The Queen's Gambit. You answer with ...e6 and keep d5.

black.why: The main break in every line: hits d4 and opens the position for your pieces.
The second break: when White's dark bishop is traded or e5 is under-defended, ...e5 frees your game completely.

plans.title: Build the house
steps: ...Be7 (vs Bg5) or ...Bd6 (vs Bf4/Bd3).
Castle before doing anything else.

plans.title: Break with ...c5
steps: Play ...c5 to hit d4.
Develop the b8-knight to c6 to add pressure.
If White takes on c5, recapture with the bishop and you are fully developed.

plans.title: Free the bad bishop
steps: ...b6 and ...Bb7, or
after an exchange on d5 (...exd5), use the c8-h3 diagonal: ...Bf5 or ...Bg4.

opponent_plans.title: Kingside attack with Bd3, Ne5, f4
steps: White aims everything at h7.
Answer: keep a knight on f6 (or f8 later), trade the Ne5 knight, and break with ...c5 in the centre.

opponent_plans.title: Central space with e4
steps: In the Colle White prepares e4.
Answer: ...c5 first, then ...Qc7 to control e5 and e4.

traps.title: Don't take on g3 too early in the London
traps.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. Bf4 Nf6 3. e3 c5 4. c3 Nc6 5. Nd2 e6 6. Ngf3 Bd6 7. Bg3 O-O 8. Bd3 Bxg3 9. hxg3
traps.explanation: After ...Bxg3 hxg3 the h-file opens for White's rook and Bxh7+ ideas get stronger. Leave the tension; let White decide.

if_deviates.why: Queen's Gambit Declined: same pawns, same plans.
Against quiet systems hit d4 with the c-pawn.
If you don't know the opening, build the house and castle. The plans come from the structure.

mistakes_to_avoid: Playing ...Nc6 before ...c5 against quiet systems: it blocks your only pawn break.
Leaving the king in the centre to grab a pawn.
Moving the f6-knight away when White has Bd3 and Qc2 aimed at h7.
Forgetting about the c8-bishop: plan ...b6/...Bb7 or ...Bf5/...Bg4 before the middlegame starts.

quiz.question: Black to move. Which pawn break is Black's main plan in this system?
quiz.explanation: **...c5** hits d4 and opens lines. It is the same break against the London, Colle, QGD and flank openings.

quiz.question: Why switch from 2...Nc6 (Chigorin style) to ...e6 / ...c5 setups?
choices: ...Nc6 blocks the c-pawn, so you lose the ...c5 break and play without a plan
quiz.explanation: The knight on c6 sits in front of the c-pawn. Without ...c5 Black has no natural way to fight for the centre, and the position becomes passive.

quiz.question: White plays a setup you've never seen. What do you do?
quiz.explanation: Build the house, castle, then break with ...c5. The structure gives you the plan.

quiz.question: Where does the dark-squared bishop go against the London (Bf4)?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. Bf4 Nf6 3. e3 c5 4. c3 Nc6 5. Nd2 e6 6. Ngf3
quiz.explanation: **...Bd6** offers a trade of White's best piece. If White takes, ...Qxd6 and ...e5 follow.

sources: Sielecki, Keep It Simple: 1.d4 (for White's setups)

pr-early-queen.title: Punishing the early queen (Scotch 4...Qh4 / 4...Qf6)
pr-early-queen.anchor: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qh4
extra_anchors: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qf6
pr-early-queen.summary: Black's queen comes out on move 4 to hit e4 or d4. Answer the threat, then develop with tempo. Every time you attack the queen, you gain a move.

goals.white: Meet the threat, develop fast, and use moves like Nb5, Nc3 and Be2-f3 that attack the queen or c7.
goals.black: Win a pawn (e4) or force White's knight back, then develop before White can punish the queen.

structure.name: Open centre: e4 pawn vs no Black centre pawn
structure.description: Black has no pawn in the centre, so lines are open. Open positions reward the side with more pieces out. That is why tempo matters so much here.

pieces.why: Defends e4 and heads for b5 or d5 to hit c7.
Blocks nothing, guards g4 and can go to f3 to hit the queen on e4.
Castle quickly. Then Re1 opens the e-file against Black's king and queen.

key_squares.why: Nb5 or Nd5 attacks it, forking king and rook if Black isn't careful.
The pawn Black's queen wants. Defend it with Nc3 or give it for a big lead.

white.why: Later, pushing e5 gains space and kicks a knight from f6.

black.why: Black's freeing move to open lines for the c8 bishop.

plans.title: Against 4...Qh4: Nc3, Be2, castle; Nb5 if Black takes e4
steps: 5.Nc3 defends e4 with development (best, about +0.8).
After 5...Bb4 6.Be2 Qxe4 7.Nb5! threatens Nxc7+. Black must play ...Bxc3+ and ...Kd8, losing castling rights.
Castle, Re1, Bf3: every move hits the queen or the king.

plans.title: Against 4...Qf6: save the knight, then develop
steps: The d4 knight is attacked twice. Play 5.Nf3, 5.Nb5 or 5.Nxc6.
Then Nc3, Be2 or Bd3, castle. The queen on f6 blocks Black's g8 knight from its best square.

opponent_plans.title: Black wins e4 and holds on
steps: If you forget about e4, Black just takes it with check-like threats on e2/e1.
Answer: make sure each move defends e4 or creates a bigger threat.

traps.title: Natural development drops the knight
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qf6 5. Bc4 Qxd4
traps.explanation: 5.Bc4?? ignores the threat. The d4 knight was attacked twice and defended once. Always ask what their last move threatens.

if_deviates.why: Develop and block the bishop's pressure on d4 and f2. The engine rates White clearly better.

mistakes_to_avoid: Answering 4...Qf6 with a developing move that leaves d4 hanging.
Spending moves chasing the queen with pawns (g3, h3) instead of developing pieces.

quiz.question: 4...Qh4 attacks e4. What is the best reply?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qh4
quiz.explanation: 5.Nc3 develops a piece and defends. 5.Qd3 brings your own queen out early, and 5.Bd3?? cuts the queen's defence of d4: 5...Nxd4 wins a piece. (5.f3 isn't even legal: the queen on h4 pins the f2 pawn.)

quiz.question: Black just took on e4. What wins time?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qh4 5. Nc3 Bb4 6. Be2 Qxe4
quiz.explanation: 7.Nb5! threatens the fork on c7. Black has to give up the bishop and move the king. 7.O-O?? is a blunder: 7...Qxd4 wins the knight, because the c6 knight also attacks d4.

quiz.question: After 4...Qf6, which move is a blunder?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qf6
quiz.explanation: 5.Bc4?? leaves d4 attacked twice and defended once: 5...Qxd4 wins a piece.

sources: Hellsten, Mastering Opening Strategy (development and tempo)

scotch-3d6.title: Scotch: 3...d6 (Black keeps e5) 4.d5
scotch-3d6.anchor: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 d6
scotch-3d6.summary: Black holds e5 with a pawn, Philidor-style, but the knight on c6 is in the way. **4.d5! kicks it with tempo and grabs space. Then c4, Nc3, castle short, and break with c5. Black's only counterplay is ...f5.**

goals.white: Gain space with d5 and c4, then open the queenside with c5 where you have more room.
goals.black: Re-route the knight (e7-g6), play ...f5 to attack your centre from the side, and attack your king on the kingside.

structure.name: Closed centre: d5/e4 vs d6/e5
structure.description: A King's Indian-type structure. The centre is locked. You attack on the queenside (c4-c5), where your pawns point; Black attacks on the kingside with ...f5, where Black's pawns point.

pieces.why: Supports e4 and c5 later. Can jump to b5 to hit c7 and a7.
d3 guards e4 against ...f5; e2 if you plan Nd2-c4.
e3 supports c5; g5 pins a knight on f6.
Black's pieces are cramped behind the d6-e5 chain.

key_squares.why: Your pawn break. It opens the c-file against c7 and d6.
Black's break. Answer ...f5 with exf5 or by keeping e4 with Nc3 and Bd3.

white.why: Opens the queenside where you have space.
Ways to meet ...f5: keep e4, or take and use e4 for a knight.

black.why: Black's main idea against e4.
Undermines d5, rarely good for Black.

plans.title: Space, then c5
steps: 4.d5 Nce7 5.c4: two pawns side by side in the centre.
Nc3, Be2 or Bd3, O-O.
Prepare c5 with Be3 or b4, then cxd6 to open the c-file.

plans.title: Meet ...f5
steps: After ...f5, Nc3 holds e4. If Black takes ...fxe4, retake with the knight: it lands on a great central square.
Or take exf5 and put a knight on e4.

opponent_plans.title: Kingside counterplay with ...f5
steps: ...Nce7-g6, ...Nf6, ...f5, sometimes ...f4 and ...g5.
Your answer: play fast on the queenside and keep e4 controlled.

traps.title: 4...Nd4? loses a pawn
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 d6 4. d5 Nd4 5. Nxd4 exd4 6. Qxd4
traps.explanation: The knight jump looks active, but after the trade d4 is just a free pawn.

traps.title: 4...Nb4 5.a3: the knight goes to the rim
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 d6 4. d5 Nb4 5. a3 Na6
traps.explanation: Black's knight is badly placed on a6. Later Bxa6 doubles Black's pawns. (5...Nxd5?? 6.exd5 just wins a piece.)

if_deviates.why: The knight went home: Black has lost time. Same plan.
Kick the knight to the rim. Later Bxa6 ruins Black's pawns.
Wins a clean pawn.
Same plan. Stockfish likes c5 soon.

mistakes_to_avoid: 4.dxe5?! dxe5 5.Qxd8+ is not bad, but 4.d5 gains much more.
Castling long: your pawns and plans are on the queenside, so castle short.
Ignoring ...f5: keep e4 covered (Nc3, Bd3) before you start the queenside play.

quiz.question: Black defended e5 with 3...d6. What is your best move?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 d6
choices: 4.d5, kick the knight and gain space
quiz.explanation: 4.d5 gains space with tempo. Every knight retreat is worse than c6.

quiz.question: Pawns are locked: d5/e4 vs d6/e5. On which side do you play?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 d6 4. d5 Nce7 5. c4 f5 6. Nc3
quiz.explanation: Play where your pawns point: c4-c5 opens the c-file. Black will play on the kingside.

quiz.question: Black tried 4...Nd4. What do you play?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 d6 4. d5 Nd4
quiz.explanation: 5.Nxd4 exd4 6.Qxd4 wins a clean pawn.

sources: Flores Rios, Chess Structures (King's Indian structure)

scotch-bc5.title: Scotch Classical: 4...Bc5 5.Nxc6
scotch-bc5.anchor: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Bc5
extra_anchors: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Bc5 5. Nxc6 Qf6
scotch-bc5.summary: Black's bishop hits d4 and f2. You answer 5.Nxc6: the attacked knight disappears and Black must choose a recapture. **The one thing to remember: after 5...Qf6 Black threatens Qxf2 mate, so 6.Qd2! (Kasparov's move). Then Nc3-a4 to trade off the c5-bishop, castle, and push f4-e5.**

goals.white: Trade on c6, guard f2, remove Black's strong c5-bishop (Na4 or Be3), castle, then use the kingside pawn majority with f4 and e5.
goals.black: Keep the c5-bishop aimed at f2, develop fast, and use the open d-file or ...d5 for counterplay.

structure.name: Scotch Classical after Nxc6
structure.description: After ...dxc6 Black has a healthy-looking but doubled queenside (four pawns that cannot make a passed pawn) and you have a 4-vs-3 kingside majority: your long-term trump is f4 and e5. After ...bxc6 Black keeps central pawns and can play ...d5, but the a7 and c6 pawns are weak.

pieces.why: Guards f2 against ...Qxf2. On d2 she can later go to f4, a5 or e3.
Na4 hits the c5-bishop: trade it and you get the bishop pair.
Guards e4, blocks the d-file from Black's rook, and aims at the kingside.
Be3 offers to trade the c5-bishop. Do not play Be3 when ...Bxe3 fxe3 wrecks you and loses time (6.Be3? in the 5...Qf6 line).

key_squares.why: Black's target. It must be guarded twice when Black's queen and bishop aim at it.
Black's best piece lives here. Na4 or Be3 to trade it.
Your pawn majority's goal square: f4 and e5 gain space.

white.why: Uses the kingside majority, kicks a knight from f6 and opens lines toward Black's king.
Kicks a bishop from d4.

black.why: After ...bxc6, Black's main break against e4.
Sometimes against your e4 pawn after Black castles long.

plans.title: Guard f2, then grab the bishop pair
steps: 5...Qf6 6.Qd2 dxc6 7.Nc3: f2 is safe.
Na4 attacks the c5-bishop. If it is traded, you have two bishops.
Bd3, O-O, c3 to kick a bishop from d4.

plans.title: Kingside majority: f4 and e5
steps: After ...dxc6 your four kingside pawns face three.
Castle short, then f4 and e5 to gain space and kick the f6 knight.
This is your plan for the whole middlegame and for the endgame too.

plans.title: Queen trade after ...dxc6
steps: If Black recaptures 5...dxc6 straight away, play 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8.
Black cannot castle. Develop with Nc3, Bf4 or Bg5+ and O-O-O with check.

opponent_plans.title: Attack f2
steps: ...Qf6 or ...Qh4 together with the c5-bishop hit f2.
Answer: Qd2 or Qe2, or castle short so the rook guards f2.

opponent_plans.title: Use the d-file
steps: After ...dxc6 Black puts a rook on d8 against your queen on d2.
Answer: Bd3 blocks the file, and castling gets the king off e1.

traps.title: Mate on f2
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Bc5 5. Nxc6 Qf6 6. Nc3 Qxf2#
traps.explanation: Queen plus bishop on f2. Any move except one that guards f2 (Qd2, Qf3, Qe2) loses on the spot.

traps.title: 6.Be3? Bxe3
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Bc5 5. Nxc6 Qf6 6. Be3 Bxe3 7. fxe3 dxc6
traps.explanation: You played this a lot. Black trades bishops, your pawns are doubled on e3, and Black still takes back on c6. Stockfish: Black is better (about -0.9).

traps.title: 5...Bxf2+? just loses a piece
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Bc5 5. Nxc6 Bxf2+ 6. Kxf2 Qf6+ 7. Qf3 bxc6
traps.explanation: The 'attack' runs out of pieces. Block the check with Qf3, and you are a piece for a pawn up.

if_deviates.why: Develop and guard e4. If 6...Qh4, 7.Qe2 guards f2, then Be3 to trade the c5-bishop.
Black's king loses castling rights. Bf4 or Bg5+ and O-O-O+ follow.
Same plan: develop, then f4 and e5.
Black's queen is exposed on c6. Develop with tempo.

mistakes_to_avoid: 6.Be3? after 5...Qf6: 6...Bxe3 7.fxe3 dxc6 and Black is better.
Leaving f2 with only the king guarding it when Black's queen and bishop aim there.
Pushing e5 before you have castled and played f4: the pawn can drop to ...Qxe5 or ...Re8.
Allowing the c5-bishop to live forever. Na4 or Be3 trades it.

quiz.question: Black threatens something. What, and how do you stop it?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Bc5 5. Nxc6 Qf6
quiz.explanation: Queen and bishop both hit f2: 6...Qxf2 would be mate. 6.Qd2 guards f2 and keeps queens on.

quiz.question: Why does White play Na4 in this line?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Bc5 5. Nxc6 Qf6 6. Qd2 dxc6 7. Nc3 Be6 8. Na4
choices: To trade off Black's strong c5-bishop
quiz.explanation: The c5-bishop is Black's best piece. Trading it gives you the bishop pair and removes the pressure on f2.

quiz.question: After ...dxc6 the pawns are: White a2 b2 c2 e4 f2 g2 h2, Black a7 b7 c7 c6 f7 g7 h7. Where is your long-term plan?
choices: Kingside: f4 and e5 with the majority
quiz.explanation: You have four pawns against three on the kingside. Push f4 and e5. Black's four queenside pawns are doubled and cannot make a passed pawn.

quiz.question: Black played 5...dxc6 (no ...Qf6). What is the simplest move?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Bc5 5. Nxc6 dxc6
quiz.explanation: After 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8 Black cannot castle. You develop with Nc3, Bf4 and O-O-O+ and have the easier endgame.

scotch-big-idea.title: The Scotch: the big picture (3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4)
extra_anchors: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4
1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 d6
1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Ne5
1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Bb4+
1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nge7
scotch-big-idea.summary: 3.d4 opens the centre at once. After 3...exd4 4.Nxd4 you have the only centre pawn (e4), more space and free development. **Your recipe in almost every line: trade on c6 when the d4 knight is attacked, develop fast, castle, then use the e4 pawn: push e5 (or f4-e5) to kick Black's knight from f6.**

goals.white: Use the extra centre pawn on e4 and the lead in development: develop, castle, then push e5 (often with f4 first) to gain space and drive Black's pieces back.
goals.black: Hit the d4 knight and the e4 pawn with pieces (...Bc5, ...Qf6, ...Nf6), then break with ...d5 to get rid of your e4 pawn and equalise.

structure.name: Open Scotch: White e4 pawn vs Black d-pawn
structure.description: After 4.Nxd4 both sides have lost the d-pawn and e-pawn pair. White keeps e4, Black keeps d7. The e4 pawn gives White more space. Black's freeing move is ...d5; if Black gets it in safely, the position is equal. If you trade on c6 and Black recaptures with the b-pawn, Black gets doubled c-pawns but also a pawn that supports ...d5.

pieces.why: A great central knight, but Black can attack it with ...Bc5, ...Qf6 or ...Nxd4. When it is attacked twice, trade it on c6.
On d4 after ...Nxd4 the queen is central and safe. In the Mieses she goes to e2 to support the e5 pawn.
d3 guards e4 and aims at Black's king; c4 hits f7 when Black is slow.
Developed early; f4 supports the e5 push. In the Mieses it goes to b2 or a3.
Castle long when your queen sits on d4 or d2 (rook to d1 at once); short in the slower lines.

key_squares.why: Your target square. A pawn on e5 kicks the f6 knight and cramps Black.
Black's freeing square. If Black gets ...d5 in with no problems, the game is level. Keep it covered with e4, c4 and Nc3.
Black's favourite target (...Bc5 and ...Qf6 or ...Qh4). Always check whether f2 is safe.

white.why: Kicks the f6 knight and gains space; usually prepared by f4 or a queen on d4/e2.
Supports e5 and kicks pieces from e5 and g5.
In the Mieses: kicks the d5 knight and stops ...d5 for good.

black.why: The main freeing break. It attacks e4 and opens the c8-bishop.
Strikes at e5 after you push it.

plans.title: Trade on c6, develop, push e5
steps: If the d4 knight is attacked (by ...Bc5, ...Qf6, ...Nf6, ...d6), take on c6. Black's pawns get doubled.
Develop: Nc3, Bd3 or Be2, castle.
Then f4 and e5, gaining space and kicking the f6 knight.

plans.title: Queen in the centre, castle long, pawn storm
steps: If Black trades on d4 (4...Nxd4 5.Qxd4), keep the queen on d4.
Nc3, Bf4 or Be3, O-O-O: the rook arrives on d1.
Then f3, g4, h4 and g5 at Black's castled king.

plans.title: Punish odd third moves
steps: If Black does not take on d4, ask: is e5 now undefended? Can I gain space with d5?
Kick the c6 knight with d5, or take on e5 when it is free.

opponent_plans.title: Black hits d4 and f2
steps: ...Bc5 and ...Qf6 attack the d4 knight twice and aim at f2.
Answer: trade on c6, and guard f2 with Qd2 (or Qe2/O-O).

opponent_plans.title: Black frees with ...d5
steps: Black wants ...d5 to trade off your e4 pawn.
Answer: keep d5 covered with Nc3 (and c4 in the Mieses), or push e5 first.

traps.title: 4...Qh4 5.Nxc6? loses e4
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qh4 5. Nxc6 Qxe4+
traps.explanation: Against 4...Qh4 your 'take on c6' habit fails: the queen takes e4 with check. Play 5.Nc3 first.

traps.title: The f2 mate in the Classical
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Bc5 5. Nxc6 Qf6 6. Nc3 Qxf2#
traps.explanation: After 4...Bc5 5.Nxc6 Qf6 Black threatens mate on f2. Only a move that guards f2 (6.Qd2 or 6.Qf3) is safe.

if_deviates.why: Black is passive. Trade on c6, develop and play f4-e5.
The knight on e5 is a target. f4 kicks it with tempo.
Gain a tempo on the bishop; if 5...Bc5, 6.Nxc6 and 7.Bd3.
A passive set-up. Develop and castle long; h4-h5 hits a knight on g6.

mistakes_to_avoid: Moving the d4 knight backwards for no reason (Nb3, Nf3) when you could trade on c6.
Forgetting f2: after ...Bc5 and ...Qf6/...Qh4, check every move whether f2 is attacked twice.
Pushing e5 when it is not protected. Push it only when the queen (d4/e2) or f4 holds it.
Leaving your king in the centre. Castle by move 8-10.

quiz.question: Black just played 4...Bc5, attacking your knight on d4. What is your simple answer?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Bc5
quiz.explanation: Trade on c6. Black must recapture with a pawn (damaging the structure) or play 5...Qf6, after which 6.Qd2 guards f2.

quiz.question: What is Black's main freeing pawn break in the Scotch?
quiz.explanation: ...d5 attacks your e4 pawn and frees the c8-bishop. Keep d5 covered with Nc3 and, in the Mieses, c4.

quiz.question: 4...Qh4 attacks e4. Which move is correct?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qh4
quiz.explanation: 5.Nc3 guards e4 and develops. 5.Nxc6? Qxe4+ loses the pawn with check.

quiz.question: Your central pawn on e4 is your trump. What is the most common way to use it?
choices: Push it to e5 to kick the f6 knight
Trade it with exd5 as soon as possible
quiz.explanation: e5 (often after f4, or with the queen on d4/e2 protecting it) gains space and drives Black's knight away from its best square.

scotch-mieses.title: Scotch: Mieses Variation (4...Nf6 5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.e5)
scotch-mieses.anchor: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nxc6 bxc6 6. e5
extra_anchors: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6
scotch-mieses.summary: Kasparov's weapon. Trade on c6, then kick the f6 knight with e5. **The e5 pawn is your whole game: protect it with Qe2, kick the d5 knight with c4, guard c4 with b3, and keep the clamp. Black's doubled c-pawns and cramped pieces are long-term problems.** You have played 6.Nc3 here; 6.e5 is more ambitious and gives clear plans.

goals.white: Keep the e5 pawn, gain space with c4, develop the bishops (b2 or a3, g2 or e2), castle, and later push f4 to support e5 or open the f-file.
goals.black: Undermine e5 with ...d6 or ...f6, use the open b-file and the a6-bishop against c4, and free the game with ...d5.

structure.name: Mieses: e5 wedge vs doubled c-pawns
structure.description: White pawn on e5 (plus c4 later); Black has doubled c-pawns (c6, c7) and an isolated a-pawn. The e5 pawn takes d6 and f6 from Black's pieces. If Black ever plays ...d5 and you take exd6, Black's pawns become loose; if you keep e5, Black stays cramped.

pieces.why: Unpins and defends e5 against ...Qe7. She blocks the f1-bishop for a while; that is the price.
On g2 it presses the long diagonal against c6 and a8.
b2 supports e5 on the long diagonal; a3 hits Black's dark squares and the f8-bishop/e7-queen.
d2 supports c4 and can go to f3 or e4; c3 if the d5 knight has left.

key_squares.why: Your pawn wedge. Everything protects it.
Black's knight's outpost. c4 kicks it away for good.
Black's ...Ba6 and ...Nb6/...Qe6 aim at it. b3 protects it.

white.why: Kicks the d5 knight and stops ...d5 for a while.
Supports e5. Later f5 can open lines toward Black's king.

black.why: Hits e5. If you take exd6, Black opens lines and the queens often come off.
Hits e5 from the other side. Usually answered by keeping the pawn with f4 or taking exf6 when Black's king is weak.
Frees Black's bishop and challenges c4.

plans.title: Main line clamp: Qe2, c4, b3, Bb2
steps: 6...Qe7 7.Qe2 Nd5 8.c4: the knight goes.
8...Ba6 pins c4 to your queen: 9.b3 protects c4.
Bb2 (or Ba3), g3 and Bg2, castle. Then f4 to support e5.

plans.title: Kasparov's knight route: 8...Nb6 9.Nd2
steps: 9.Nd2 protects c4 and stays flexible.
b3, Bb2, then O-O-O or O-O. f4 supports e5.

plans.title: Endgame: Black's pawns are the weakness
steps: After queens come off, Black's a-pawn and doubled c-pawns are targets.
Your extra space and the e5 wedge give a long, safe edge.

opponent_plans.title: Hit e5 with ...d6 or ...f6
steps: Black challenges the wedge.
Keep it with f4, or take and use your better structure.

opponent_plans.title: Pressure c4
steps: ...Ba6, ...Nb6, ...Qe6 all hit c4.
b3 and Nd2 protect it.

traps.title: 9.cxd5?? Bxe2
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nxc6 bxc6 6. e5 Qe7 7. Qe2 Nd5 8. c4 Ba6 9. cxd5 Bxe2
traps.explanation: c4 is pinned to your queen by the a6-bishop. Taking the knight loses the queen. Play 9.b3.

traps.title: 7...Bb4+ 8.Bd2 Qe7?? 9.cxd5
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nxc6 bxc6 6. e5 Nd5 7. c4 Bb4+ 8. Bd2 Qe7 9. cxd5
traps.explanation: Black hopes for ...Qxe5+, but after 10.Qe2 the pins break and White is a piece up.

traps.title: 6...Ng8? wastes time
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nxc6 bxc6 6. e5 Ng8
traps.explanation: Not a trick, a gift: the knight goes home. Develop fast with Bd3, O-O, Qe2, f4.

if_deviates.why: Black's king loses castling rights. Develop with Bd2 or Bg5, then O-O-O with check and f3.
Trade the active knight. Your e5 pawn stays.
Kick it. 7...Nb6 8.Bd3; 7...Bb4+ 8.Bd2.
Block with the knight. It supports c4 and the queen on b4 achieves little.

if_deviates.answer: Bb2 or Ba3, g3, Bg2, castle
if_deviates.why: Same plan. Kasparov met 9...g6 with 10.f4 f6 11.Ba3.

mistakes_to_avoid: Taking cxd5 while the a6-bishop pins c4 to your queen on e2.
Letting e5 drop: after ...Qe7, the pawn is pinned, so play Qe2 before anything else.
Rushing exd6 when Black plays ...d6: you open lines for Black's bishops. Keep e5 with f4 if you can.
6.Nc3 instead of 6.e5: it is fine, but it gives Black an easy ...d5 and you lose the Mieses plans.

quiz.question: Black pinned your e5 pawn with 6...Qe7. What now?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nxc6 bxc6 6. e5 Qe7
quiz.explanation: The e5 pawn is pinned against your king, so 7.exf6 is illegal. 7.Qe2 defends e5 and unpins.

quiz.question: Black played 8...Ba6, pinning c4. Best move?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nxc6 bxc6 6. e5 Qe7 7. Qe2 Nd5 8. c4 Ba6
quiz.explanation: 9.b3 protects c4 so the pin does nothing. 9.cxd5?? Bxe2 loses the queen.

quiz.question: What is the most important feature of the Mieses for White?
quiz.explanation: e5 takes f6 and d6 from Black's pieces. Every white move supports it.

quiz.question: Black played 6...Nd5 instead of 6...Qe7. Your move?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nxc6 bxc6 6. e5 Nd5
quiz.explanation: 7.c4 kicks it out of the centre and gains space. After 7...Nb6 develop with 8.Bd3 and castle.

scotch-odd-third.title: Scotch: Black's odd third moves (3...f6, 3...d5, 3...Nf6 and others)
scotch-odd-third.anchor: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 f6
extra_anchors: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 d5
1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 Nf6
1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 Bd6
1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 Bb4+
1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 f5
1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 Qf6
1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 Nxd4
scotch-odd-third.summary: When Black does not take on d4, ask two questions: **Is e5 now free to take? Can d5 kick the c6 knight?** One of them almost always works. Against moves that weaken the king (3...f6, 3...f5), open lines and check on h5.

goals.white: Win the e5 pawn or gain space with d5, then develop fast. Punish king weaknesses with Bc4 and Qh5+.
goals.black: Survive the opening with a solid centre, or create confusion with an early counter-strike.

structure.name: Various: mostly open centres
structure.description: After dxe5 or Nxe5 the centre opens and your faster development counts. After d5 the centre is closed and you have space.

pieces.why: Against ...f6 or ...f5, it aims at g8 and f7: Black's king cannot castle easily.
When Black's f-pawn moved, Qh5+ is the key attacking move.
Develop with Nc3; a knight on e5 is often the reward for taking the pawn.

key_squares.why: Black's pawn there often lost its defender. Take it.
After ...f6 or ...f5, the e8-h5 diagonal is open.
Weak after ...f6: Bc4 and Ng5 hit it.

white.why: Opens the position when Black's king is weak.
Kicks the c6 knight and gains space.

black.why: Black's freeing move in many of these lines.

plans.title: 3...f6: open up and hit f7
steps: 4.dxe5 fxe5 5.Bc4: the bishop eyes g8 and f7.
6.Ng5 attacks f7 twice. Black must find ...d5.
If 4...Nxe5 5.Nxe5 fxe5?? 6.Qh5+ wins material.

plans.title: 3...Nf6, 3...Bd6, 3...d5: take and develop
steps: 3...Nf6 4.dxe5 Nxe4 5.Qe2 Nc5 6.Nc3: then Be3 or Bg5 and O-O-O.
3...Bd6 4.dxe5 Nxe5 5.Nxe5 Bxe5 6.f4: kick the bishop.
3...d5 4.Nxe5 dxe4 5.Bb5: pin, take on c6, castle, win e4.

plans.title: 3...Bb4+ and 3...Qf6: kick with d5
steps: 3...Bb4+ 4.c3 Ba5 5.d5 Nce7 6.Nxe5: a free pawn.
3...Qf6 4.d5 Nce7 5.Nc3, then Bg5 hitting the queen.

opponent_plans.title: Counter-strike in the centre
steps: ...d5 or ...f5 tries to open lines before you are developed.
Answer: take what is offered (e5), develop with checks and threats.

traps.title: 3...f6: 5...fxe5?? 6.Qh5+
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 f6 4. dxe5 Nxe5 5. Nxe5 fxe5 6. Qh5+ g6 7. Qxe5+
traps.explanation: The queen forks king and h8 rook. 6...Ke7 7.Qxe5+ Kf7 8.Bc4+ is no better.

traps.title: 3...f5: 6...g6?? 7.Qe5+
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 f5 4. Nxe5 fxe4 5. Nxc6 bxc6 6. Qh5+ g6 7. Qe5+
traps.explanation: Same fork idea: check on e5 and the h8 rook falls.

traps.title: 3...Bb4+ 4.c3 exd4?: 5.cxb4
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 Bb4+ 4. c3 exd4 5. cxb4
traps.explanation: The c3 pawn is pinned, but it can still capture the pinning bishop. White wins a piece for two pawns.

traps.title: 3...Qf6 4.d5 Nd4: don't play 6.Qxd4??
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 Qf6 4. d5 Nd4 5. Nxd4 exd4 6. Bd3
traps.explanation: 6.Qxd4?? Qxd4 loses your queen: the f6 queen guards d4. 6.Bd3 develops, and the d4 pawn is weak.

if_deviates.why: This is the same position as 4...Nxd4 5.Qxd4. Same plan: Nc3, Bf4, O-O-O.
Develop and hit g8/f7. exf6 and Qd5 ideas follow.
Black's king loses castling rights and the e4 pawn is weak.
Protect e5. The knight on g4 achieves nothing.
Ask the two questions: is e5 free? does d5 kick the knight?

mistakes_to_avoid: Playing on autopilot (Nxd4) when Black did not take on d4: check if e5 is free first.
Grabbing on d4 with the queen when Black's queen on f6 defends d4.
Forgetting to develop after winning a pawn: castle first, then cash in.

quiz.question: Black played 3...f6. What is the strongest reply?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 f6
choices: 4.dxe5, opening lines toward the weak king
quiz.explanation: 4.dxe5 opens the position. If 4...fxe5 5.Bc4 eyes f7; if 4...Nxe5 5.Nxe5 fxe5?? 6.Qh5+ wins.

quiz.question: Black checked with 3...Bb4+ and you blocked with 4.c3. Black played 4...Ba5. What now?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 Bb4+ 4. c3 Ba5
choices: 5.d5, kick the knight and win e5
quiz.explanation: 5.d5 Nce7 6.Nxe5: the knight left, so e5 is free.

quiz.question: Black played 3...d5. What is White's simplest good move?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 d5
quiz.explanation: e5 is no longer defended by a pawn. 4.Nxe5 dxe4 5.Bb5 pins the c6 knight, and the e4 pawn will be weak.

quiz.question: Black played 3...Nf6. Which move fits your plan?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 Nf6
choices: 4.dxe5, then Qe2 to chase the knight
quiz.explanation: 4.dxe5 Nxe4 5.Qe2 Nc5 6.Nc3: you develop with tempo and the e5 pawn cramps Black.

scotch-queen-sorties.title: Scotch: early queen sorties (4...Qf6 and 4...Qh4)
scotch-queen-sorties.anchor: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qf6
extra_anchors: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qh4
scotch-queen-sorties.summary: Black's queen comes out on move 4 to attack your knight (...Qf6) or your e4 and f2 pawns (...Qh4). **Rule: against ...Qf6 trade on c6 and develop with tempo on the queen; against ...Qh4 do NOT take on c6 (...Qxe4+), play 5.Nc3 and develop, even if it costs the e4 pawn.**

goals.white: Develop with tempo against the exposed queen, castle quickly, and use your lead in development (Nc3-d5 or b5, Re1, e5).
goals.black: Win a pawn (e4) or tie you down to f2, then catch up in development.

structure.name: Open centre, early queen
structure.description: Same open Scotch centre: your e4 pawn against Black's d7 pawn. The difference is Black's queen, which is out early and becomes a target for your minor pieces.

pieces.why: Defends e4 and jumps forward with threats against c7 and the black queen.
d3 guards e4; e2 in the ...Qh4 gambit line, so you can castle quickly.
Castle short early: the rook then guards f2 and goes to e1.

key_squares.why: Black's target in the ...Qh4 line. Defend it with Nc3 and Bd3, or give it for a big lead in development.
After Nb5 the fork Nxc7+ hits king and rook.
Hit by ...Qf6/...Qh4 with ...Bc5. Castling or Qd2 guards it.

white.why: Gains time on a queen on f6 or c6 and opens lines.
Knight jumps that hit c7 and the queen.

black.why: Black's freeing move once the queen sortie is over.

plans.title: Against 4...Qf6: trade on c6 and develop
steps: 5.Nxc6. If 5...Qxc6, 6.Bd3 and 7.O-O, then Nc3 and Nd5 or Re1 and e5.
If 5...dxc6, 6.Bd3, O-O, then f4-e5 with the kingside majority.
If 5...Bc5, 6.Qd2: the same position as the 4...Bc5 line.

plans.title: Against 4...Qh4: develop, even for a pawn
steps: 5.Nc3 Bb4 6.Be2: castling is near.
If 6...Qxe4 7.Nb5! threatens Nxc7+. After 7...Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 Kd8 9.O-O, Black's king is stuck.
Then Re1, Bf3, Bg5+ and Nd4: everything toward the black king.

opponent_plans.title: Win e4
steps: ...Qh4, ...Bb4 and ...Qxe4 pick up the pawn.
Black pays with time and a king in the centre.

opponent_plans.title: Trade queens
steps: ...Qf6 can offer a queen trade on d4 or f3 to kill your initiative.
Keep queens when your development lead is big; trade them when Black's pawns are broken.

traps.title: 5.Nxc6? Qxe4+
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qh4 5. Nxc6 Qxe4+
traps.explanation: The usual trade fails here: Black takes e4 with check. 5.Nc3 first.

traps.title: 5...Nf6? 6.Ndb5
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qh4 5. Nc3 Nf6 6. Ndb5
traps.explanation: The knight threatens Nxc7+ forking king and rook. Black must give up castling with ...Kd8 or lose material. (6.g3 or 6.Nf5, hunting the queen, are even stronger.)

traps.title: The Nb5 fork in the gambit line
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qh4 5. Nc3 Bb4 6. Be2 Qxe4 7. Nb5
traps.explanation: Nxc7+ is threatened. Black's best is 7...Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 Kd8 9.O-O: a pawn down, you have two bishops, open lines and a black king stuck in the centre.

if_deviates.why: Same position as 4...Bc5 5.Nxc6 Qf6: guard f2.
Develop and block the bishop. f2 is safe and Nb5 or Nf5 can follow.
Castle; your lead in development is big (Stockfish about +1.9). If 7...Bxc3, first 8.Nf5! hitting the queen, then recapture on c3.

mistakes_to_avoid: Playing 5.Nxc6 against 4...Qh4: the e4 pawn falls with check.
Running around to keep the e4 pawn instead of castling in the ...Qh4 line.
Forgetting f2: if Black adds ...Bc5, guard f2 (Qd2, Be3, or castle).

quiz.question: Black played 4...Qh4. Your usual 5.Nxc6 fails. Why, and what instead?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qh4
quiz.explanation: 5.Nxc6 Qxe4+ loses e4 with check. 5.Nc3 guards e4 and develops.

quiz.question: In the gambit line Black grabbed e4. What is the point of your next move?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qh4 5. Nc3 Bb4 6. Be2 Qxe4
quiz.explanation: 7.Nb5 attacks c7: Nxc7+ would fork king and rook. Black's best is to give up the bishop on c3 and move the king.

quiz.question: After 4...Qf6 5.Nxc6 Qxc6, which plan fits?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qf6 5. Nxc6 Qxc6
choices: Bd3, O-O, Nc3: develop with gains of time on the queen
quiz.explanation: Black's queen is exposed on c6. Develop and castle; Nc3-d5 and e5 will hit it again.

quiz.question: After 4...Qf6 5.Nxc6, Black played 5...Bc5. What now?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Qf6 5. Nxc6 Bc5
quiz.explanation: Qxf2 mate is threatened. 6.Qd2 guards f2; this is the main 4...Bc5 position.

scotch-qxd4.title: Scotch: 4...Nxd4 5.Qxd4 (queen in the centre)
scotch-qxd4.anchor: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nxd4 5. Qxd4
scotch-qxd4.summary: Your most common position (over 300 of your games). Black's trade brings your queen to a dominant central square that no black minor piece can attack. **Set-up: Nc3, Bf4 (or Bd2/Be3), O-O-O, then f3 and a g4-h4 pawn storm. If Black plays ...Nf6, check whether e5 kicks it.**

goals.white: Keep the queen on d4, develop with Nc3 and Bf4, castle long, and attack Black's king with pawns (f3, g4, h4) while the d1 rook hits d6/d7.
goals.black: Gain time on your queen (...c5, ...Bc5 after ...b6, ...Nf6-e6) and free the game with ...d5 or a queen trade with ...Qf6.

structure.name: Open centre, White e4 vs Black d-pawn
structure.description: Only one knight per side is left. White's e4 pawn gives space. If Black plays ...d6, the d6 pawn is a fixed target on the half-open d-file. If Black plays ...c5, the d5 square becomes a permanent hole.

pieces.why: Central, eyes g7 and a7, guards e4 and e5. Retreat to e3 only if a pawn (...c5) kicks her.
Guards e4. Jumps to d5 when Black's pawns leave it (after ...c5).
Presses d6 and c7, supports e5. Use d2 or e3 if ...Bc5/...Nh5 make f4 awkward.
After O-O-O it is on the open d-file at once, against d6/d7.
Develop it after castling; c4 hits f7 if Black is careless.

key_squares.why: A hole if Black plays ...c5. Put a knight there.
Push e5 when Black's knight is on f6 and your queen protects the pawn.
The queen on d4 eyes it; Qg3 or Qe3-g3 hits it in some lines.

white.why: Kicks the f6 knight. In this line the queen protects e5, so it is often possible at once (5...Nf6 6.e5!).
The pawn storm after opposite castling. f3 first keeps e4 safe.

black.why: Gains a tempo on the queen but leaves a hole on d5.
Frees Black's game. Keep it under control with Nc3 and the rook on d1.

plans.title: Castle long and storm
steps: Nc3, Bf4, O-O-O: rook to d1 at once.
f3 to make e4 solid.
g4, h4, g5 to open lines at Black's king.

plans.title: Kick the knight with e5
steps: If Black's knight goes to f6 before ...d6, push e5.
The queen protects e5. The knight has no good square: d5 and g4 lose to the queen.
Develop with Nc3, Bf4, O-O-O with a big lead.

plans.title: Use the d5 hole after ...c5
steps: Retreat the queen to e3 (it watches the e-file and g5).
Nc3-d5, castle long, and press the backward d6 pawn.

opponent_plans.title: Gain time on the queen
steps: ...c5, ...Bc5 (after ...b6) or ...Nf6-e6 hit the queen.
Answer: move her once to a good square (e3 or d2) and keep developing.

opponent_plans.title: Trade queens with ...Qf6
steps: Black offers the trade to kill your attack.
Answer: 6.e5! gains space; after 6...Qb6 7.Qxb6 axb6 you have the better endgame.

traps.title: 6...Nd5?? 7.Qxd5
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nxd4 5. Qxd4 Nf6 6. e5 Nd5 7. Qxd5
traps.explanation: The knight on d5 is attacked by the queen and nothing defends it.

traps.title: 6...Ng4?? 7.Qxg4
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nxd4 5. Qxd4 Nf6 6. e5 Ng4 7. Qxg4
traps.explanation: With the e4 pawn gone to e5, the 4th rank is open: the queen slides across to g4.

traps.title: 6...Qe7 7.Be3! and the knight is stuck
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nxd4 5. Qxd4 Nf6 6. e5 Qe7 7. Be3
traps.explanation: ...Qe7 pins e5 for a moment, but 7.Be3 unpins and now exf6 is threatened. The knight has no safe square (Nd5 Qxd5, Ng4 Qxg4, Nh5 g4) and White is close to winning.

traps.title: 6...Qxe5+?? after 5...Qf6 6.e5
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nxd4 5. Qxd4 Qf6 6. e5 Qxe5+ 7. Qxe5+
traps.explanation: e5 is protected by your queen. Grabbing it just loses Black's queen.

if_deviates.why: Same set-up. Nc3 protects e4 from the b7-bishop in advance.
Black wants ...Nc6 with tempo. Let it come: 6...Nc6 7.Qe3 and keep developing.
The queen on e7 blocks Black's bishop. Develop and castle long.
Black prepares ...d5. Your rook on d1 and Nc3 make that break hard.

mistakes_to_avoid: Moving the queen again and again. One retreat (e3 or d2) when hit by a pawn, then develop.
6.Qxf6 after 5...Qf6: it develops Black's knight with tempo and gives an equal endgame. Prefer 6.e5.
Castling short here. Long castling puts the rook on d1 at once and lets your pawns storm.
Forgetting f3 before g4: e4 can hang when the g-pawn advances.

quiz.question: Black played 5...Nf6. What is your strongest reply?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nxd4 5. Qxd4 Nf6
quiz.explanation: 6.e5! The queen protects e5, and the knight has no good square: 6...Nd5?? 7.Qxd5 and 6...Ng4?? 7.Qxg4.

quiz.question: After 5...d6 6.Nc3 Nf6 7.Bf4 Be7, where does your king go?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nxd4 5. Qxd4 d6 6. Nc3 Nf6 7. Bf4 Be7
quiz.explanation: Long castling puts the rook on d1 against d6 and lets your kingside pawns storm with f3, g4, h4.

quiz.question: Black hit your queen with 5...c5. What does that move weaken?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nxd4 5. Qxd4 c5
quiz.explanation: No black pawn can ever cover d5 again. Retreat 6.Qe3, then Nc3-d5.

quiz.question: Opposite castling: you on c1, Black on g8. What is the plan?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nxd4 5. Qxd4 d6 6. Nc3 Nf6 7. Bf4 Be7 8. O-O-O O-O
quiz.explanation: With opposite castling the faster attack wins. f3 makes e4 solid, then g4-g5 kicks the f6 knight and opens lines.

st-advance.title: Structure: the advance chain (Caro-Kann Advance)
st-advance.summary: White's pawns d4-e5 form a chain pointing at your kingside. White has space; you have a solid position and, unlike the French, your light-squared bishop is already outside the chain on f5. Your plan: attack the base of the chain with ...c5, pile up on d4 with ...Nc6 and ...Qb6, and only later think about ...f6.

goals.white: Use the space: kingside expansion (g4, h4, f4-f5), keep d4 supported (c3, Nf3, Be3), sometimes c4 to open the queenside.
goals.black: Hit the base: ...c5, ...Nc6, ...Qb6 (and ...Ne7-f5) against d4. Keep the f5 bishop safe from g4/h4 hunts.

structure.name: Advance chain: d4-e5 vs c6/c5-d5-e6
structure.description: White: d4 and e5 (often c3 too). Black: d5 and e6, with the c-pawn going ...c6-c5. White's chain points at the kingside, so White attacks there; Black's chain (d5-e6) points at the queenside, so Black plays there. The rule from Nimzowitsch: attack a chain at its base. White's base is d4.

pieces.why: Your 'good' bishop, outside the chain. Keep it safe from g4/h4 and Nh4.
Both aim at d4. A knight on f5 is ideal: it hits d4 and blocks White's kingside play.
Hits d4 and b2.
Inside the chain, this is the 'bad' bishop. Trade it or activate it after ...cxd4.
Supports d4; after ...cxd4 Nxd4 it becomes a strong centre knight.

key_squares.why: The base of White's chain: Black's main target.
A great square for a Black knight (after ...Ne7) or bishop.
The head of the chain. ...f6 attacks it, but that weakens e6.

white.why: Opens the queenside and the c-file; can leave Black's d5 isolated.
Kingside space and an attack on e6.
Hunts the f5 bishop and gains kingside space.

black.why: The main break: attacks the base of the chain.
Attacks the head. Good later, once d4 is under fire, but it weakens e6 and the light squares.

plans.title: Attack the base: ...c5, ...Nc6, ...Qb6
steps: Play ...e6 and ...c5 (c6-c5 costs a tempo, but it is the right lever).
Add ...Nc6 and ...Qb6, and ...Ne7-f5 for a third attacker on d4.

plans.title: Trade the bad bishop or put it outside
steps: After ...cxd4 cxd4, the e7 bishop can go to b4 with check.
Or trade it for a White knight or bishop when possible.

plans.title: Later: ...f6 against the head
steps: Once White's centre is under pressure, ...f6 can open the f-file for your rook.
Do it only when your king is safe and e6 is guarded.

opponent_plans.title: Kingside expansion and bishop hunt
steps: White plays Nc3, g4 and h4 to trap or harass the f5 bishop.
Answer: keep an escape (...h6, ...Bh7) or play ...c5 at once to counter in the centre.

opponent_plans.title: The blockade (Nimzowitsch)
steps: White gives up d4 (dxc5) and puts pieces on d4 and e5 instead.
Answer: develop quickly and get ...e5 or ...f6 in before the blockade is complete.

if_deviates.answer: Retreat ...Bg6, then hit the centre with ...c5 and kick with ...h5 if g4/h4 overreach.
if_deviates.why: When White overextends on the kingside, a central counter is the cure.

if_deviates.answer: 4...h5 (or 4...h6) to stop h5 trapping your bishop.
if_deviates.why: Stop the bishop hunt before it starts.

mistakes_to_avoid: Playing ...e6 before ...Bf5. Then the bishop is shut inside the chain, like a bad French.
Never playing ...c5. Without it you have no counterplay at all.
Playing ...f6 too early: it weakens e6 and the king.
Letting the f5 bishop be trapped by g4, h4 and h5.

quiz.question: Black to move. What is the key pawn break?
quiz.explanation: Nimzowitsch's rule: attack a chain at its base. ...c5 hits d4 and opens lines for your pieces.

quiz.question: Which White pawn is the base of the chain?
quiz.explanation: The chain is d4-e5. The rear pawn, d4, is the base; it supports everything.

quiz.question: Why is the Caro-Kann Advance easier for Black than the French Advance?
choices: The light-squared bishop is outside the chain on f5
quiz.explanation: In the French, ...e6 comes first and the c8 bishop is shut in. In the Caro, ...Bf5 comes before ...e6.

sources: Flores Rios, Chess Structures: A Grandmaster Guide (French/Caro advance chains)

st-carlsbad.title: Structure: Carlsbad (QGD Exchange)
st-carlsbad.anchor: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. cxd5 exd5
extra_anchors: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 d5 4. cxd5 exd5
1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. cxd5 exd5 5. Bg5 c6 6. e3
st-carlsbad.summary: When White takes cxd5 and you recapture exd5, you get the Carlsbad: your pawns on a7-b7-c6-d5 face White's a2-b2-d4-e3. White plays on the queenside (the minority attack b4-b5) or in the centre (f3 and e4). You play on the kingside and on e4, and you trade your light-squared bishop.

goals.white: Minority attack (b4-b5xc6) to leave Black a weak pawn, or the central break f3 + e4.
goals.black: Trade the light-squared bishops (...Bf5), use the e4 square (...Ne4) and attack on the kingside before White's queenside play bites.

structure.name: Carlsbad: d4+e3 vs c6+d5
structure.description: White: a2, b2, d4, e3, f2, g2, h2. Black: a7, b7, c6, d5, f7, g7, h7. White has the half-open c-file and a 2-vs-3 queenside (the minority). Black has the half-open e-file, a strong outpost on e4, and more room on the kingside. Black's light-squared bishop is the piece that can become bad behind d5, so Black likes to trade it with ...Bf5.

pieces.why: e4 is Black's outpost, supported by d5. The other knight goes d7-f8-g6 to defend and attack the kingside.
Trade it for White's good bishop on d3. If it stays behind d5 it can be a bad piece.
The half-open e-file and the e4 square belong to Black.
They support b4-b5 and press on c6/c7.
White's best minor piece, aimed at h7. Black wants to trade it.

key_squares.why: Black's outpost: a knight on e4 is hard to remove and supports kingside play.
The target of the minority attack. After b5xc6 bxc6 it is backward on a half-open file.
After b5xc6 bxc6, c5 is a hole for a White knight.
Where Black's bishop goes to trade off White's d3 bishop.

white.why: The minority attack: break up Black's queenside pawns and leave a weak c6 or d5.
The central plan (Botvinnik): a mobile centre and a kingside attack.

black.why: The kingside plan: a knight on e4 backed by ...f5 (a Stonewall-like setup) and a kingside attack.
Only when White's pieces are not ready to hit an isolated d5 pawn. It gives Black active pieces.
Meet the minority attack: ...a6 and ...b5 can block it, ...a5 can slow b4.

plans.title: Trade the light-squared bishops with ...Bf5
steps: Play ...c6 and ...Bf5 early, before White plays Qc2 and Bd3 to stop it.
If White takes on f5, your worst piece is gone.

plans.title: The e4 outpost and kingside attack
steps: Knight to e4, the other knight to g6 via d7-f8.
Rook to e8, queen to f6 or h4, bishop to d6 aiming at h2.
Sometimes ...f5 supports the knight and adds a rook lift ...Rf6-h6.

plans.title: Meet b4-b5 calmly
steps: If White plays b5, often answer ...cxb5 only when your pieces can hit d4 and the c-file; otherwise let White take bxc6 and recapture with the b-pawn.
Keep a knight ready for c4 or e4 and counter on the kingside.

opponent_plans.title: The minority attack
steps: White plays Rb1, b4, a4 and b5, then bxc6.
Result: a backward pawn on c6 (or an isolated d5), a hole on c5, and rooks hitting c6.

opponent_plans.title: The central break f3 and e4
steps: White puts a knight on e2, plays f3 and e4, opening lines for a kingside attack.
Answer: keep pieces on e4 and d5, or strike first with ...c5.

if_deviates.answer: Use ...g6 and ...Bf5 later, or ...Nh5 and ...g6 to prepare it; otherwise play ...Ne4 and ...f5.
if_deviates.why: Qc2 watches f5. You still want to trade that bishop sooner or later.

if_deviates.answer: Attack on the queenside with ...b5-b4 and ...a5.
if_deviates.why: With opposite-side castling, pawn storms decide.

mistakes_to_avoid: Playing passively while White plays b4-b5. Always have a plan on the kingside.
Leaving your c8 bishop at home behind d5 all game.
Taking ...cxb5 without thinking: it can leave an isolated d5 pawn on an open file.
Playing ...c5 when White's pieces are ready to hit an isolated d5 pawn.

quiz.question: Black to move. What does Black's light-squared bishop want to do?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. cxd5 exd5 5. Bg5 c6 6. e3
choices: ...Bf5, to trade it for White's best bishop
quiz.explanation: The c8 bishop can get stuck behind d5. Developing it to f5 while the diagonal is open is the simplest equaliser.

quiz.question: White plays b4 and b5. What is the target?
quiz.explanation: After b5xc6 bxc6, c6 is backward on the half-open c-file and c5 becomes a hole for a White knight.

quiz.question: Which square is Black's outpost in the Carlsbad?
quiz.explanation: d5 guards e4, and only f2-f3 can kick a knight from there.

quiz.question: White played Nge2 and f3. What is White planning?
quiz.explanation: The knight on e2 and pawn on f3 both support e4. This is Botvinnik's central plan.

sources: Flores Rios, Chess Structures: A Grandmaster Guide (Carlsbad chapter)

st-caro-slav-centre.title: Structure: d4 vs c6+e6 (Caro Classical / Scandinavian)
st-caro-slav-centre.anchor: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. Nc3 dxe4 4. Nxe4 Bf5 5. Ng3 Bg6
extra_anchors: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. Nc3 dxe4 4. Nxe4 Bf5 5. Ng3 Bg6 6. h4 h6 7. Nf3 Nd7 8. h5 Bh7 9. Bd3 Bxd3 10. Qxd3 e6
1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Qxd5 3. Nc3 Qa5 4. d4 Nf6 5. Nf3 c6
st-caro-slav-centre.summary: After ...dxe4 (Caro Classical) or ...Qxd5 (Scandinavian), White keeps a pawn on d4 and Black sets up c6+e6. White has more space and the e5 square; Black is very solid and waits for the right moment to strike with ...c5 (or ...e5). You play Black in the Caro version and White in the Scandinavian version.

goals.white: Use space and e5: knight on e5, kingside space (h4-h5 in the Caro), long castling and a kingside attack, or c4 and d5 to open the centre.
goals.black: Finish development (bishop out before ...e6!), castle, then break with ...c5 to trade White's d4 pawn. Trade pieces when cramped.

structure.name: Semi-open centre: d4 vs c6 + e6
structure.description: White: d4 plus the a-, b-, c-, f-, g-, h-pawns (no e-pawn). Black: c6 and e6 plus the a-, b-, f-, g-, h-pawns (no d-pawn). White controls e5 and has more space. Black has no weaknesses, and the two breaks ...c5 and ...e5 will free the position. Flores Rios calls this the Slav / Caro-Kann formation.

pieces.why: Develop it before ...e6. In the Caro main line it is traded on d3.
The d7 knight controls e5 and supports ...c5 or ...e5.
Supports ...c5/...e5 and watches e5.
The outpost in front of Black's position.
Opposite-side castling means pawn storms.

key_squares.why: White's outpost. Black covers it with ...Nd7 and ...Qc7.
White's c4-d5 break hits it; Black's pieces like it too.
Black's main break square.

white.why: Opens the centre for White's better-placed pieces.
Kingside space and a pawn storm (when kings are castled on opposite sides).

black.why: The main break: trades the d4 pawn and frees Black's game.
The other freeing break, usually prepared with ...Nd7 and ...Qc7.

plans.title: Develop, castle, then ...c5 (Black)
steps: Bishop out first (...Bf5/...Bg6), then ...e6, ...Nd7, ...Ngf6, ...Be7 (or ...Bd6), castle.
Play ...c5 (or ...Qc7 and ...e5) to trade White's d4 pawn.

plans.title: Trade to relieve the cramp (Black)
steps: Trade White's e5 knight with ...Nxe5 or ...Nd7.
Trade the light-squared bishops on d3.

plans.title: Space and attack (White)
steps: Knight to e5, queen to e2 or d3, castle long.
Push the kingside pawns, or play c4 and d5 to open the centre.

opponent_plans.title: White's kingside attack (when you are Black)
steps: In the Caro main line White castles long and pushes g4-g5.
Answer: strike in the centre with ...c5 at once; a central break is the best defence against a flank attack.

opponent_plans.title: Black's ...c5 or ...e5 (when you are White in the Scandinavian)
steps: Black finishes development and breaks with ...c5 or ...e5.
Answer: be ready to meet it with d4-d5 or with active pieces (Bd2, Qe2, O-O-O, Ne5).

if_deviates.answer: 8.Nd5! hits the a5 queen (discovered by Bd2) and f6.
if_deviates.why: A typical tactic: the Bd2 and Nc3 line up against the queen on a5.
Same structure, same plan.

mistakes_to_avoid: As Black: playing ...e6 before the bishop is out (it is locked in).
As Black: never playing ...c5 or ...e5, so White's space slowly squeezes you.
As White: letting Black play ...c5 for free with all pieces developed.
As White (Scandinavian): forgetting the queen on a5 can be hit by Nd5 or b4 tactics.

quiz.question: Black is fully developed. What is Black's main pawn break?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. Nc3 dxe4 4. Nxe4 Bf5 5. Ng3 Bg6 6. h4 h6 7. Nf3 Nd7 8. h5 Bh7 9. Bd3 Bxd3 10. Qxd3 e6 11. Bd2 Ngf6 12. O-O-O Be7 13. Kb1 O-O 14. Ne4
quiz.explanation: ...c5 is the standard freeing break. It hits d4 and opens the c-file toward White's king on b1.

quiz.question: Which square is White's outpost in this structure?
quiz.explanation: d4 supports e5, and only ...f6 could challenge a knight there, which weakens e6. Black covers it with ...Nd7 and ...Qc7.

quiz.question: White to move (Scandinavian). What is the tactical shot?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Qxd5 3. Nc3 Qa5 4. d4 Nf6 5. Nf3 c6 6. Bc4 Bf5 7. Bd2 e6
choices: 8.Nd5, uncovering Bd2 on the queen and hitting f6
quiz.explanation: The c3 knight leaves with tempo: Bd2 now attacks the a5 queen, and Nd5 hits f6 and c7. After 8...Qd8 9.Nxf6+ Qxf6 White has a clear lead in development (engine: about +0.9).

sources: Flores Rios, Chess Structures: A Grandmaster Guide (Slav / Caro-Kann formation)
Hanging Pawns, Caro-Kann and Scandinavian structure videos

st-iqp.title: Structure: the isolated queen's pawn (Panov / QGD)
st-iqp.anchor: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. c4 Nf6 5. Nc3 e6 6. Nf3 Be7 7. cxd5 Nxd5
extra_anchors: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. c4 Nf6 5. Nc3 e6 6. Nf3 Be7 7. cxd5 Nxd5 8. Bd3 Nc6 9. O-O O-O
st-iqp.summary: In the Panov (and many QGD lines) White ends up with an isolated pawn on d4: no c- or e-pawn next to it. The IQP side gets free piece play and attacking chances; the defender gets a permanent target and a perfect blockade square on d5. Middlegame: IQP side attacks. Endgame: the defender wins.

goals.white: Attack before the pieces come off: Ne5, a battery on h7 (Bc2 + Qd3), a rook lift, and the d4-d5 break.
goals.black: Blockade d5 with a piece, trade pieces (especially White's attackers), keep the king safe, then win the d4 pawn in the ending.

structure.name: IQP: White pawn on d4, no c- or e-pawns
structure.description: White: a2, b2, d4, f2, g2, h2. Black: a7, b7, e6, f7, g7, h7. The d4 pawn controls e5 and c5 (outposts for White's knights) but can never be defended by a pawn. The square in front of it, d5, can never be attacked by a White pawn: it is the perfect blockade square for Black.

pieces.why: The ideal blockader: it stops d4-d5 and cannot be kicked by a pawn.
Adds control of d5 from the long diagonal.
Guards h7 and d5. Do not move it away while White's battery points at h7.
The c-file is open and d4 is the target.
The IQP side's best attacking piece, supported by d4.
The battery against h7.

key_squares.why: Black's blockade square. Whoever controls d5 controls the game.
White's outpost for a knight.
The weakness. In an ending it falls.

white.why: The IQP break. It opens lines when White's pieces are ready, often with tactics on e6 and f7.

black.why: Black's 'break' is piece play: blockade d5, trade pieces, then pile up on d4.
Only in special cases to trade the isolated pawn.

plans.title: Blockade d5 (Black)
steps: Keep a knight on d5. Add ...b6 and ...Bb7 to control d5 again.
Never let d4-d5 happen with tempo.

plans.title: Trade pieces (Black)
steps: Every trade helps the defender: fewer attackers, a weaker d4 in the ending.
Good trades: ...Nxc3 (when it leaves White's pawns weak), ...Nb4 to trade the d3 bishop, ...Bf6 against Ne5.

plans.title: Pile up on d4 (Black)
steps: Rooks on d8 and c8, ...Nc6, ...Bf6: hit d4 with more pieces than White can defend with.
In an ending the isolated pawn usually falls.

opponent_plans.title: Ne5 and a kingside attack (White)
steps: Knight to e5, bishop to c2, queen to d3: mate threats on h7.
A rook lift Re3-g3/h3 and the f-pawn (f4-f5) add more.

opponent_plans.title: The d4-d5 break (White)
steps: When Black's blockade is weak, d5 opens the centre: exd5 Nxd5 or a pin on the e-file.
Answer: always count attackers and defenders on d5.

if_deviates.move: White plays Bg5 to pin the f6 knight
if_deviates.why: Trading the pinning bishop for the knight would weaken your control of d5 and h7.

if_deviates.move: White avoids the IQP (e.g. c5 with a queenside majority)
if_deviates.answer: Hit the c5 chain with ...b6 or ...e5.
if_deviates.why: That pawn chain is overextended.

mistakes_to_avoid: As the defender: leaving d5 unguarded, so d4-d5 blows the position open.
As the defender: moving the f6 knight away when White has Bc2 and Qd3 on h7.
As the IQP side: trading pieces. Every trade brings you closer to a lost ending.
As the IQP side: playing passively. The IQP is only good if you attack.

quiz.question: Which square should Black occupy with a piece in the IQP structure?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. c4 Nf6 5. Nc3 e6 6. Nf3 Be7 7. cxd5 Nxd5
choices: d5, the square in front of the pawn
quiz.explanation: d5 can never be attacked by a White pawn. A piece there stops d4-d5 and is a rock.

quiz.question: Do trades help the IQP side or the defender?
quiz.explanation: The IQP's strength is piece activity. With fewer pieces the pawn is just weak, and in the ending it falls.

quiz.question: What is the IQP side's typical pawn break?
quiz.explanation: d4-d5 opens lines when the blockade is weak; often it comes with tactics on e6 and f7.

quiz.question: White has Bc2 and Qd3. Which of your pieces must not leave its post?
choices: The f6 knight, which guards h7
