quiz.explanation: The Bc2 + Qd3 battery threatens Qxh7 mate. The f6 knight is the main guard.

sources: Flores Rios, Chess Structures: A Grandmaster Guide (IQP chapter)

st-london.title: Structure: the London / Colle pyramid (d4-e3-c3)
st-london.anchor: 1. d4 d5 2. Bf4 Nf6 3. e3 e6 4. Nf3 c5 5. c3 Nc6
extra_anchors: 1. d4 d5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Bf4 e6 4. e3 c5 5. c3 Nc6
1. d4 d5 2. Bf4 Nf6 3. e3 e6 4. Nf3 c5 5. c3 Nc6 6. Nbd2 Bd6 7. Bg3 O-O 8. Bd3
st-london.summary: Against the London (and Colle) White builds a solid pyramid: c3, d4, e3. The dark-squared bishop goes out to f4 first, which leaves b2 without its natural defender. Your setup: ...d5, ...e6, ...c5, ...Nc6, then ...Qb6 against b2/d4, ...Bd6 to trade the London bishop, and later ...e5 or ...c4.

goals.white: Solid centre, Ne5 with f4 (a Stonewall-style attack), the Bd3 + Qc2 battery against h7, and sometimes dxc5 followed by e4.
goals.black: Pressure d4 and b2 (...c5, ...Nc6, ...Qb6), trade the f4 bishop with ...Bd6, keep h7 safe, then free the game with ...e5 or gain queenside space with ...c4 and ...b5.

structure.name: London pyramid: c3-d4-e3 vs c5-d5-e6
structure.description: White: a2, b2, c3, d4, e3, f2, g2, h2. Black: a7, b7, c5, d5, e6, f7, g7, h7. The centre is locked in the middle; the fight is about d4 and e5. Black's c5 pawn and pieces hit d4; White's pieces aim at e5 and Black's king. Black's light-squared bishop is the problem piece behind e6, so Black plays ...b6/...Bb7 or ...Bd7, or frees it with ...e5.

pieces.why: Hits b2 and d4 at the same time. White must spend a move defending.
Offers the trade of White's best piece, the London bishop.
c6 hits d4; f6 guards h7. The f6 knight can go to d7 to fight for e5.
The problem piece. Get it out via ...b6/...Bb7, or free it with ...e5.
White's dream square, often backed by f4.

key_squares.why: Undefended once the bishop goes to f4. ...Qb6 targets it.
White's outpost and the square of Black's freeing break ...e5.
The target of White's Bd3 + Qc2 battery and the Greek-gift Bxh7+.

white.why: A Stonewall-like clamp on e5 and a kingside attack.
Opens the centre when Black's pieces are badly placed.

black.why: The freeing break: frees the c8 bishop and fights for the centre. Prepare with ...Qc7, ...Re8 or ...Nd7.
Gains queenside space and kills the Bd3; then ...b5-b4. Only good when White cannot hit back with e4.

plans.title: Hit b2 and d4: ...Qb6
steps: With the bishop on f4, b2 is loose. ...Qb6 hits b2 and adds to the pressure on d4.
White must play Qb3, Qc2 or Qc1, or give up b2.

plans.title: Trade the London bishop: ...Bd6
steps: Offer ...Bd6. If White trades on d6, the bishop that controls e5 is gone.
If White retreats Bg3, you can still trade it or meet Ne5 calmly.

plans.title: Free the position: ...e5 (or ...c4 and ...b5)
steps: Prepare ...e5 with ...Qc7, ...Re8 or ...Nd7. After ...e5 your c8 bishop is free.
Or play ...c4, then ...b5-b4 to attack c3.

opponent_plans.title: Ne5, f4 and a kingside attack
steps: White plants a knight on e5, supports it with f4 and swings the queen and rook toward your king.
Answer: trade the e5 knight (...Nd7, ...Nxe5) and keep the f6 knight near h7.

opponent_plans.title: The h7 battery and Greek gift
steps: Bd3 + Qc2 aim at h7. If your f6 knight is chased away, Bxh7+ may come.
Answer: keep a knight on f6, or play ...h6 or ...g6 before castling into trouble.

if_deviates.move: White plays Nc3 and e4 ideas (Jobava London)
if_deviates.why: The same pressure on d4 works; just watch for Nb5 jumps.

if_deviates.move: White plays the Colle (Bd3 and e3 without Bf4)
if_deviates.why: Without Bf4, e5 is easier for you; ...e5 is the main freeing move.

mistakes_to_avoid: Castling short and then moving the f6 knight away while Bd3 and Qc2 point at h7.
Allowing a knight on e5 to stay forever with f4 behind it.
Leaving the c8 bishop at home all game.
Playing ...c4 when White can answer e3-e4 and blow the centre open.

quiz.question: Black to move. White's bishop left c1 early. Which pawn is now weak?
quiz.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. Bf4 Nf6 3. e3 c5 4. c3 Nc6 5. Nd2
quiz.explanation: The c1 bishop used to guard b2. ...Qb6 hits b2 and d4 at once, and White has to find a defence.

quiz.question: Why does Black play ...Bd6 against the London?
choices: To trade White's best piece, the f4 bishop
quiz.explanation: The London bishop controls e5 and b8. Trading it makes White's Ne5 plans weaker.

quiz.question: Which pawn break frees Black's position in the London structure?
quiz.explanation: ...e5 fights for the centre and frees the c8 bishop. Prepare it with ...Qc7 or ...Re8.

quiz.question: White has Bd3 and Qc2. What must Black remember?
choices: Keep h7 protected (knight on f6, or ...h6/...g6)
quiz.explanation: The battery aims at h7. If the f6 knight goes, Bxh7+ ideas appear.

sources: Flores Rios, Chess Structures: A Grandmaster Guide
Sielecki, Keep It Simple: 1.d4 (Black's lines vs the London)

st-reversed-carlsbad.title: Structure: reversed Carlsbad (Caro-Kann Exchange)
st-reversed-carlsbad.anchor: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Bd3
extra_anchors: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Bd3 Nc6 5. c3 Nf6 6. Bf4 Bg4 7. Qb3
st-reversed-carlsbad.summary: The Caro-Kann Exchange gives the Carlsbad with colours reversed: White has c3+d4 against Black's d5+e6 (or e7). Now Black owns the minority (a- and b-pawn vs three) and plays ...b5-b4. White owns the e5 outpost, the half-open e-file and attacking chances on the kingside. You play both sides of this one.

goals.white: Use e5 and the kingside: Bd3, Bf4, Nf3-e5, Qc2 or Qb3, sometimes f4. Keep Black's light-squared bishop from a good trade.
goals.black: Develop the light-squared bishop before ...e6 (...Bg4 or ...Bf5), trade dark-squared bishops with ...Bd6, then the minority attack ...b5-b4.

structure.name: Reversed Carlsbad: c3+d4 vs d5+e6
structure.description: White: a2, b2, c3, d4, f2, g2, h2. Black: a7, b7, d5, e6 (or e7), f7, g7, h7. The c-file is half-open for Black, the e-file for White. White's outpost is e5, Black's is c4 (and e4 is contested). A tempo up compared with the QGD, White has the more natural kingside chances.

pieces.why: Aims at h7 and controls f5 so Black's bishop cannot trade on f5 easily.
Controls e5 and b8. Black tries to trade it with ...Bd6.
Qb3 hits b7 when Black's bishop has left c8; Qc2 backs up the d3 bishop.
A knight on e5 is White's best piece in this structure.
Black must develop it before ...e6, or it is shut in.

key_squares.why: White's outpost, covered by d4 and Bf4. Only ...f6 can chase a knight from there, and that weakens e6.
Black's outpost, the mirror image of e5.
Weak once Black's bishop leaves c8. Qb3 hits it.

white.why: Supports the e5 knight and prepares f5 or a rook lift. A Pillsbury-style attack.
Not a pawn break, but the main lever: pieces on the e-file and e5.

black.why: The minority attack: hit c3 to leave White a weak c-pawn or isolated d4.
Rare; only if White's pieces cannot hit an isolated d5 afterwards.

plans.title: Qb3 and pressure on b7 (White)
steps: After ...Bg4 or ...Bf5, play Qb3 and hit b7.
Black must spend a move (...Qd7, ...Qc8, ...Na5) to answer.

plans.title: Knight to e5 and a kingside attack (White)
steps: Nd2 and Ngf3, then Ne5. Castle short, rook to e1.
Bring the queen to the kingside (Qc2, Qe2, Qh5) and consider f4 or a rook lift Re3-h3.

plans.title: Minority attack ...b5-b4 (Black)
steps: Trade dark-squared bishops with ...Bd6, castle, put rooks on b8 and c8.
Push ...b5 and ...b4 to hit c3.
After ...bxc3 bxc3, White's c3 pawn is backward on the half-open c-file.

opponent_plans.title: Black (when you are White): ...Bg4, ...Bd6, ...b5-b4
steps: Black develops the bishop before ...e6, trades dark-squared bishops and pushes the b-pawn.
Answer: be faster on the kingside; keep the e5 square under control.

opponent_plans.title: White (when you are Black): Ne5, f4 and a kingside attack
steps: White puts a knight on e5, queen and bishop on the b1-h7 diagonal.
Answer: trade the e5 knight (...Nd7 or ...Nxe5) and keep a knight on f6 to cover h7.

if_deviates.answer: Qb3 or Nf3, then develop normally.
if_deviates.why: Bg4 pins nothing important; b7 is a target.

if_deviates.move: Black plays ...e6 before the bishop comes out
if_deviates.answer: Keep your plan: Nf3, O-O, Re1, Ne5.
if_deviates.why: Black's light-squared bishop is now the bad piece.

mistakes_to_avoid: As White: forgetting that ...Bf5 trades your best bishop. Bd3 plus Qc2 stops it.
As White: castling and then doing nothing while Black pushes ...b5-b4.
As Black: playing ...e6 before ...Bg4 or ...Bf5, burying the bishop.
As Black: allowing a knight on e5 to stay forever.

quiz.question: Black just played ...Bg4. What is White's most annoying move?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Bd3 Nc6 5. c3 Nf6 6. Bf4 Bg4
quiz.explanation: With the bishop gone from c8, b7 is loose. Qb3 forces Black to spend time on ...Qd7, ...Qc8 or ...Na5.

quiz.question: Who has the minority attack in the Caro-Kann Exchange structure, and how does it work?
quiz.explanation: It is a Carlsbad with colours reversed. Black's two queenside pawns (a, b) attack White's three (a, b, c).

quiz.question: Which square is White's outpost here?
quiz.explanation: d4 and Bf4 cover e5. Only ...f6 can chase a knight from there, and that weakens e6.

sources: Flores Rios, Chess Structures: A Grandmaster Guide (Carlsbad and reversed Carlsbad)
Hanging Pawns, Caro-Kann Exchange structure videos

st-scotch-structure.title: Structure: the Scotch centre (e4 vs d7/d6)
st-scotch-structure.anchor: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4
extra_anchors: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Bc5 5. Nb3 Bb6 6. a4 a6 7. Nc3 d6
st-scotch-structure.summary: After 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 the d- and e-files are half-open. White has the e4 pawn in the centre, Black has the d-pawn on d7 or d6. White owns more space; Black is solid but must free himself with ...d5 or trade pieces.

goals.white: Use the extra central pawn: gain kingside space with f4, then break with e5 or f5, and use d5 as an outpost.
goals.black: Free the position with ...d5 (or trade into an ending), pressure e4 with ...Re8 and ...Nf6, and trade White's best pieces.

structure.name: Scotch structure: e4 pawn vs d6 (or d7) pawn
structure.description: White has a pawn on e4 and no d-pawn. Black has a pawn on d6 or d7 and no e-pawn. White controls d5 and f5 and has more space. Black's d6 pawn is solid but can become a backward pawn on the half-open d-file. Whoever plays the right pawn break first takes over: e4-e5 or f4-f5 for White, ...d5 for Black.

pieces.why: The d4 knight is centralised. Its partner on c3 can jump to d5, a square no Black pawn can easily cover.
Backs up d4 and fights for c5, where Black's bishop wants to be.
d3 guards e4 and aims at the kingside; c4 hits f7 but can be hit by ...Na5 or ...d5.
The d-file pressures d6; the e-file backs up the e4-e5 push.
Hemmed in by d6. Black often trades it with ...Be6 or ...Bg4.

key_squares.why: White's outpost. A knight here hits c7, e7 and f6 and cannot be chased by a pawn unless Black plays ...c6.
White's break square. e4-e5 opens the e-file and kicks the f6 knight.
f4-f5 gains kingside space and can open the f-file toward f7.
Black's target. ...Nf6, ...Re8 and ...Bb4 (pinning the c3 knight) all hit it.

white.why: Opens the e-file and kicks the f6 knight. Prepare it with f4 and a rook on e1.
Kingside space and an attack; f5 also takes e6 from Black's pieces.

black.why: The freeing break. If Black plays ...d5 safely, the e4 pawn is traded and White's extra space is gone.
A rarer break against e4. Only good when Black's king is safe and White cannot use e6.

plans.title: Kingside space: f4, then e5 or f5
steps: Castle short, put the bishop on d3 and a rook on e1.
Play f4 to support e5 and f5.
Push e5 when it kicks a knight or opens the e-file, or f5 to cramp Black's kingside.

plans.title: The d5 outpost
steps: Put a knight on d5. It hits c7 and e7 and cannot be kicked unless Black plays ...c6.
If Black trades on d5, recapture with the pawn (exd5): the c6 knight is hit and d6 becomes a fixed target.

plans.title: Pressure on d6
steps: If Black's pawn is on d6, it can become backward on the half-open d-file.
Rooks on d1, queen on d2, knight on d5 or b5: d6 becomes a target.

opponent_plans.title: Black frees himself with ...d5
steps: Black plays ...Re8, ...Nf6 and ...c6, then ...d5.
Answer: keep enough pieces on e4 (Nc3, Bd3, Re1) so ...d5 loses a pawn or leaves Black with an isolated pawn.

opponent_plans.title: Trades and pressure on e4
steps: Black trades knights with ...Nxd4, puts a rook on e8 and a bishop on b4 pinning c3.
Answer: keep pieces on the board when you have more space; defend e4 with Bd3 and f3 if needed.

if_deviates.answer: Take on d5 (exd5) and play against the isolated or hanging pawns that remain.
if_deviates.why: Once ...d5 is in, the Scotch structure turns into an open game with isolated pawns.

if_deviates.answer: Develop with tempo (Be3, Nc3, Qd2 or Nb5).
if_deviates.why: Early queen moves in this structure lose time to your minor pieces.

mistakes_to_avoid: Pushing e5 too early, when Black can simply retreat the knight and attack e5 with ...d6 or ...Qe7.
Letting Black play ...d5 for free. Watch the d5 square every move.
Trading your d4 knight for nothing. That knight is the reason you have space.
As Black: sitting passively with ...d6 and ...Be7 and never preparing ...d5 or a piece trade.

quiz.question: White to move. Which pawn break is White's main lever in this structure?
quiz.explanation: White's pawns point to the kingside. f4 supports e4-e5 and f4-f5. Queenside pushes do nothing here.

quiz.question: What is Black's freeing break in the Scotch structure?
quiz.explanation: ...d5 trades off White's e4 pawn, and with it White's space advantage.

quiz.question: Why is d5 a great square for White's knight here?
choices: No Black pawn can attack it unless Black plays ...c6, and it hits c7, e7 and f6
quiz.explanation: Black's e-pawn is gone, so only ...c6 can ever chase a knight from d5. From there it eyes c7, e7 and f6.

sources: Flores Rios, Chess Structures: A Grandmaster Guide (the Scotch formation chapter)

wo-alapin.title: Sicilian Alapin (2.c3): two pawns in the centre, then the isolated-pawn attack
wo-alapin.summary: Instead of learning the Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov and ten other Open Sicilians, play 2.c3 and d4. You get a big centre or, very often, an isolated d4 pawn with fast, active pieces: the same open, attacking positions you like from the Scotch. One idea covers almost every Black reply.

goals.white: Play d4 and keep a strong centre. If you end up with an isolated d4 pawn, use the activity: Nc3, Bd3/Bc4, Re1, Ne5, and the d5 break or a kingside attack.
goals.black: Hit the centre at once (...d5 or ...Nf6), trade pieces and later attack your isolated d4 pawn.

structure.name: Isolated queen's pawn (IQP) on d4
structure.description: After ...cxd4 cxd4 and ...d5xe4/exd5 you have a pawn on d4 with no c- or e-pawn next to it. It is a weakness in the endgame but a strength in the middlegame: it controls e5 and c5, gives your pieces space, and supports Ne5 and the d4-d5 break.

pieces.why: The dream square, supported by the d4 pawn.
Supports d5; often hits a black queen on d5.
Aims at f7 or h7; behind the d5 break from a2.
On the half-open e-file, supports Ne5 and pressure on e6.
Battery with the bishop on h7 or support for the kingside attack.

key_squares.why: Your outpost, supported by d4.
The square of your break and Black's blockade square.
Targets of the attack (Bc4/Ba2 and Bd3 + Qd3/Qc2).

white.why: The key IQP break: open lines when your pieces are more active. Trade off Black's blockader first.

black.why: Black puts a piece on d5 and trades pieces toward an endgame.

plans.title: Attack with the IQP
steps: Nc3, Bc4/Bd3, O-O, Re1.
a3 and Ba2 (or Bc2) to keep the bishop on the long diagonal.
Ne5, Qd3, Bg5 and pieces to the kingside; sacrifices on f7 or e6 appear.

plans.title: The d5 break
steps: Line up rook on d1/e1, bishop on a2, knight on c3.
Push d5 when Black's pieces are passive.
Open lines toward e6/f7 and Black's king.

plans.title: Big centre when Black lets you
steps: Against ...d6/...g6, recapture cxd4 for e4+d4.
Nc3, Nf3, Be2, O-O, then h3, Be3 and e5 or d5.

opponent_plans.title: Blockade and trade
steps: Black puts a knight on d5 and trades pieces.
Avoid useless trades; keep knights and the attacking bishop.

opponent_plans.title: Early queen activity (...d5, ...Qxd5)
steps: Black's queen sits on d5 because Nc3 is not possible yet.
Develop Nf3, Be2, O-O; after ...cxd4 cxd4, Nc3 comes with tempo.

traps.title: The knight has no squares: 3...Ne4?
traps.explanation: After 3.e5 the knight must go to d5. On e4 it is kicked by d3 and has nowhere safe to go: ...Ng5 Bxg5, ...Nc5 d4, ...Nxf2 loses it for a pawn.

traps.title: The IQP sacrifice on f7
traps.pgn: 1. e4 c5 2. c3 Nc6 3. d4 cxd4 4. cxd4 d5 5. exd5 Qxd5 6. Nf3 e6 7. Nc3 Qd8 8. Bc4 Nf6 9. O-O Be7 10. Re1 O-O 11. a3 b6 12. Ba2 Bb7 13. Qd3 Rc8 14. Bg5 Re8 15. Rad1 Na5 16. Ne5 h6 17. Nxf7 Kxf7 18. Bxe6+ Kf8 19. Qg6
traps.explanation: Ne5 + Ba2 + Re1 point at f7 and e6. After a careless ...h6, Nxf7 and Bxe6+ smash the king: Qf7 mate is coming.

if_deviates.answer: 4.exd5 Qxd5 5.Nf3 then Be2, O-O; after ...cxd4 cxd4
if_deviates.why: Same IQP structure as the main line.
The knight raid ...Qxd1 Rxd1 Nc2 runs into Na3 and gets nothing.
Take the centre; the Dragon bishop bites on d4.
Black's d5 square is weak and d4 is still coming.
The queen gets kicked by Nc3.

mistakes_to_avoid: Playing 2.Nf3 out of habit: then you need a whole Open Sicilian repertoire.
Trading your attacking pieces (Nc3, the bishop on a2/d3) when you have the IQP.
Going into an endgame with the isolated pawn: attack in the middlegame instead.
Forgetting a3: without it, ...Nb4 or ...Bb4 annoys you.

quiz.question: Black played 2...Nf6. Your move?
quiz.explanation: e5 kicks the knight to d5, then d4 builds the centre. 3.d3 is too passive and Nc3 is impossible: your pawn is on c3.

quiz.question: You have an isolated d4 pawn. What is the right attitude?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 c5 2. c3 Nc6 3. d4 cxd4 4. cxd4 d5 5. exd5 Qxd5 6. Nf3 e6 7. Nc3 Qd8 8. Bc4 Nf6 9. O-O Be7
choices: Attack: Re1, a3, Ba2, Ne5, Qd3
Trade queens and pieces for a safe endgame
quiz.explanation: The IQP is strong in the middlegame and weak in the endgame. Use it now.

quiz.question: Which square is your knight's dream square in the IQP?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 c5 2. c3 d5 3. exd5 Qxd5 4. d4 Nf6 5. Nf3 Bg4 6. Be2 e6 7. O-O Nc6 8. Be3 cxd4 9. cxd4 Be7 10. Nc3
quiz.explanation: e5 is supported by d4 and cannot be hit by a black pawn easily (only ...f6).

quiz.question: Why play a3 and Ba2 in the IQP?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 c5 2. c3 Nc6 3. d4 cxd4 4. cxd4 d5 5. exd5 Qxd5 6. Nf3 e6 7. Nc3 Qd8 8. Bc4 Nf6 9. O-O Be7 10. Re1 O-O
choices: To keep the bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal, safe from ...Na5/...Nb4
quiz.explanation: From a2 the bishop supports d5 and hits e6/f7, and it cannot be chased by Black's knights.

lines.name: Alapin 2...Nc6: d4, Nf3, Nc3, Bc4, Re1 (IQP attack)
Alapin 2...e6: French-style structure, trade bishops, isolated d5

wo-alekhine.title: Alekhine (1...Nf6): 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3, space without overextending
wo-alekhine.anchor: 1. e4 Nf6 2. e5 Nd5 3. d4 d6 4. Nf3
extra_anchors: 1. e4 Nf6 2. e5 Nd5 3. d4 d6
wo-alekhine.summary: Black wants you to chase the knight with many pawn moves and then attack your overextended centre. The Modern Variation (4.Nf3) is the Keep-It-Simple answer: one pawn push, then normal development. Your e5 pawn cramps Black, and his knight often ends up misplaced on b6.

goals.white: Keep the e5 pawn (or swap it on your terms), develop Nf3, Bc4/Be2, O-O, h3, and harass the b6 knight with a4-a5.
goals.black: Undermine e5 with ...d6, ...dxe5 and ...Nc6, put pressure on d4 with ...Bg7 or ...Bg4.

structure.name: Space wedge on e5 (or open centre after ...dxe5 dxe5)
structure.description: If Black keeps ...d6, your e5 pawn gives you space on the kingside. If Black trades ...dxe5 and you recapture dxe5, the d-file opens and the e5 pawn becomes a wedge that cramps the black kingside.

pieces.why: Hits the d5 knight with tempo, then aims at f7 from b3.
Protects e5 a second time and supports a later Rd1.
Guards e5 and d4.
Kicks the b6 knight away from the centre.

key_squares.why: Your space pawn. Defend it with Nf3, Qe2, Re1.
Black's bishop wants to pin your Nf3 there; h3 stops it.
Where Black's knight usually ends up, far from the kingside.

white.why: Kick the d5 knight and build a big centre (vs ...Bg4 lines).
Harass the knight on b6.
Release tension only when it helps your development.

black.why: Black's main idea: open lines against e5/d4.
Hit d4.

plans.title: Short's set-up against ...g6
steps: Bc4 (tempo on Nd5), Bb3.
Qe2, O-O, h3.
a4-a5 against the b6 knight; Rd1 if the d-file opens.

plans.title: Big centre against ...Bg4
steps: Be2, O-O, c4 to kick the knight.
h3 to ask the bishop.
Nc3, Be3: a big, safe centre.

opponent_plans.title: Pressure on e5 and d4
steps: Keep e5 defended by pieces; recapture dxe5 when the d-file helps you.

traps.title: The f7 sacrifice: 5...Nd7?
traps.pgn: 1. e4 Nf6 2. e5 Nd5 3. d4 d6 4. Nf3 dxe5 5. Nxe5 Nd7 6. Nxf7 Kxf7 7. Qh5+ Ke6 8. c4
traps.explanation: ...Nd7 takes away the d7 square and leaves f7 weak. Nxf7 and Qh5+ drag the king into the centre, and c4 hunts the d5 knight.

traps.title: 2...Ne4? walks into trouble
traps.explanation: On e4 the knight has no future: d3 or f3 will kick it and it has few safe squares. Just take the centre.

if_deviates.why: Classic big centre; you are clearly better.
Your knight is strong on e5 and f7 is a target.
Black has wasted two moves.
Keep it simple: c4 + d4 centre and quick development.

mistakes_to_avoid: Pushing c4, f4 and e5 all at once (Four Pawns): too much theory and easy to overextend.
Letting ...Bg4 pin and trade your Nf3 so that e5 falls: play h3 in time.
Leaving the knight on b6 in peace: a4-a5 gains space and time.

quiz.question: 1.e4 Nf6. What is White's simplest strong move?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 Nf6
choices: 2.e5, chasing the knight and gaining space
quiz.explanation: 2.e5 gains space with tempo. Then d4 and Nf3 build a stable centre.

quiz.question: After 4...g6, which move hits the d5 knight while developing?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 Nf6 2. e5 Nd5 3. d4 d6 4. Nf3 g6
quiz.explanation: Bc4 develops with tempo. After ...Nb6 the bishop retreats to b3 and keeps aiming at f7.

quiz.question: Black's knight sits on b6. How do you harass it?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 Nf6 2. e5 Nd5 3. d4 d6 4. Nf3 g6 5. Bc4 Nb6 6. Bb3 Bg7 7. Qe2 Nc6 8. O-O O-O 9. h3
quiz.explanation: a4-a5 kicks the knight and gains queenside space, exactly as Short did against Timman.

wo-caro-exchange.title: Caro-Kann Exchange (3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3): Fischer's set-up
wo-caro-exchange.anchor: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Bd3
extra_anchors: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Bd3 Nc6 5. c3 Nf6 6. Bf4
wo-caro-exchange.summary: You trade on d5 and get a clear structure with no theory to memorise. Bd3 stops ...Bf5, Bf4 goes outside the chain, Qb3 hits b7 when the bishop leaves c8, and your play is on the kingside with Ne5 and f4. You play the Caro yourself as Black, so you know this structure from the other side.

goals.white: Develop Bd3, c3, Bf4, Nf3, Nbd2, O-O; use the e5 square and attack on the kingside (Ne5, f4-f5, Qc2/Qb1 battery on h7).
goals.black: Develop the light bishop actively, then play the minority attack ...b5-b4 against your c3 pawn.

structure.name: Carlsbad reversed (White c3+d4 vs Black d5, e6)
structure.description: White pawns on c3/d4, Black pawns on d5/e6 with the c-file open for Black and the e-file half open for you. It is the Queen's Gambit Exchange with colours reversed: Black gets a minority attack on the queenside, you get the e5 outpost and kingside play.

pieces.why: Stops ...Bf5 and later forms a battery with the queen against h7.
Goes outside the c3-d4 chain before the knights block it; controls e5 and b8.
Qb3 hits b7 and d5 when ...Bg4 leaves b7 loose. Later Qc2 or Qb1 aims at h7.
Lands on e5, the hole in Black's camp.
Supports Nf3/e5 and can go f3 or b3; the c3 pawn takes c3 from it.

key_squares.why: Your outpost. A knight on e5 supported by d4 and f4 is the heart of the attack.
Weak once Black's bishop leaves c8 for g4.
Target of the Bd3 + Qc2 battery.

white.why: With a knight on e5, f4-f5 rips open the e6 pawn and the kingside (Fischer vs Petrosian).
Rarely: attacks d5 and opens the c-file when Black's queenside has advanced.

black.why: The minority attack: trade on c3 and leave you with a weak c-pawn.
Frees Black's game but gives him an isolated d5 pawn.

plans.title: Ne5 and f4: the kingside clamp
steps: Nbd2, Ngf3, O-O.
Ne5 when it cannot be traded easily.
f4 to support it, then f4-f5 to open lines.

plans.title: Qb3 against b7
steps: When Black plays ...Bg4, Qb3 hits b7 and d5.
Black must spend a move (...Qd7, ...Na5, ...Qc8).
Then bring the queen back to c2 aiming at h7.

plans.title: Swap Black's good bishop
steps: Against ...g6 and ...Bf5, take Bxf5: Black recaptures gxf5 with broken pawns.
Against ...Bd6, trade with Bxd6: Black's best defender of the dark squares is gone.

opponent_plans.title: Minority attack ...b5-b4
steps: Meet it with a4 (as Fischer did) or by being faster on the kingside.

opponent_plans.title: ...e5 to free the position
steps: Black takes on an isolated d5 pawn for activity.
Answer dxe5, pin with Qe2, blockade d4 and win d5 later.

traps.title: Forgetting b7 after ...Bg4
traps.pgn: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Bd3 Nc6 5. c3 Nf6 6. Bf4 Bg4 7. Qb3 e6 8. Qxb7
traps.explanation: After ...Bg4 the b7 pawn has no defender. 7...e6? simply drops it and Black's position collapses (8...Rc8 9.Bb5).

traps.title: The e-file pin after ...e5
traps.pgn: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Bd3 Nc6 5. c3 e5 6. dxe5 Nxe5 7. Qe2
traps.explanation: The knight on e5 is pinned to the king. Black must break the pin with ...Qe7, or the knight falls to f4.

if_deviates.why: Same idea: hit b7. Often transposes after ...Nc6.
Develop, swap Black's dark bishop, then Ne5 and Rae1.
Trade Black's good bishop, then Ne5 and f4.
The queen stops Bf4 for a moment; develop and play Bf4 or Ng3.
Scandinavian-like: develop with tempo on the queen.

mistakes_to_avoid: Playing Nf3 before Bf4: the knight is fine, but don't let ...Bg4 and ...e6 lock your bishop in with Nbd2 first.
Ignoring the minority attack: play a4 or be faster on the kingside.
Trading on e5 so that Black's pieces get e5 instead of yours.
Moving the queen off c2/b1 when it is aiming at h7.

quiz.question: Black just played 6...Bg4. Best reaction?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Bd3 Nc6 5. c3 Nf6 6. Bf4 Bg4
quiz.explanation: With the bishop gone from c8, b7 is loose. Qb3 forces Black to spend time defending.

quiz.question: What is White's main plan in this structure?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Bd3 Nc6 5. c3 Nf6 6. Bf4 Bg4 7. Qb3 Na5 8. Qa4+ Bd7 9. Qc2 e6 10. Nf3
choices: Ne5, f4 and a kingside attack
quiz.explanation: The reversed Carlsbad gives you e5 and kingside play. The minority attack is Black's plan, not yours.

quiz.question: Black plays ...g6 and ...Bf5. What do you do?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Bd3 Nc6 5. c3 Nf6 6. Bf4 g6 7. Nf3 Bf5
quiz.explanation: After Bxf5 gxf5 Black has doubled f-pawns and a weak e5 square for your knight.

quiz.question: Black played ...e5 and took back with the knight. Which move pins it?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Bd3 Nc6 5. c3 e5 6. dxe5 Nxe5
quiz.explanation: Qe2 pins the knight against the king. Black has to play ...Qe7, and you blockade the isolated d5 pawn.

lines.name: Caro-Kann Exchange: 6...g6, swap the bishops and use e5
Caro-Kann Exchange: 5...e5, blockade the isolated pawn

wo-e5-offbeat.title: Odd second moves after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 (2...Bc5, 2...Qf6, 2...f5, 2...f6, 2...d5, 2...Qe7)
extra_anchors: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Qf6
1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Qe7
wo-e5-offbeat.summary: After 2.Nf3 most Black moves other than 2...Nc6 either leave e5 undefended or defend it badly. The rule: if e5 is free, take it (Nxe5). If Black's queen defends it, develop with tempo on the queen (Nc3, d4, Bg5). Your 2.Nf3 stays the same as in the Scotch.

goals.white: Take the e5 pawn when it is free, then develop quickly; punish early queen moves with tempo.
goals.black: Surprise you with a gambit or a trap, and get quick piece play for the pawn.

structure.name: Open centre, extra pawn
structure.description: In most of these lines you are a pawn up with an open centre. Develop, castle, and trade pieces: the extra pawn wins the endgame.

pieces.why: Takes the loose e5 pawn.
Hits a queen on f6/e7 and the c7 pawn.
Develops with tempo on a queen on f6.

key_squares.why: Undefended after 2...Bc5, 2...f5, 2...d5.
After ...f6 or ...f5 the king's diagonal is open: Qh5+ wins.

white.why: Open the centre while Black's pieces are badly placed.

black.why: Black's usual attempt to free himself after a gambit.

plans.title: Take e5, then develop
steps: Nxe5 against 2...Bc5, 2...f5, 2...f6.
d4 to defend the knight or gain tempo.
Nc3, Bd3/Bc4, O-O.

plans.title: Hit the early queen
steps: Against 2...Qf6/2...Qe7: Nc3, then d4 and Bg5 or Nd5.
Never block your development to chase the queen with pawns.

opponent_plans.title: Gambit pressure on f2 and e4
steps: ...Bc5/...Bxf2+ tricks, ...Qh4 checks, ...fxe4 in the Latvian.

wo-french.title: French Exchange (3.exd5 exd5 4.Bd3): win the race for the e-file
wo-french.anchor: 1. e4 e6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 exd5 4. Bd3
extra_anchors: 1. e4 e6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 exd5
wo-french.summary: The Exchange takes away everything French players like: no locked pawn chain, no ...c5 and ...f6 against your centre, no bad bishop for Black but also no theory for you. The position is symmetric, so the side that develops better and grabs the open e-file first gets the edge. You move first: Bd3, Nf3, O-O, Re1, Bg5.

goals.white: Develop quickly (Bd3, Nf3, O-O), take the e-file with Re1, pin with Bg5, then aim the Bd3 + Qc2 battery at h7 or use the e5 square.
goals.black: Copy your development, contest the e-file with ...Re8, or play ...c5 and accept an isolated d5 pawn for activity.

structure.name: Symmetric French Exchange (open e-file)
structure.description: Pawns d4 vs d5, no e-pawns. The e-file is fully open and both e5 and e4 are outposts. Small things decide: who controls the e-file, who has the more active bishops, and whether Black ends up with an isolated d-pawn after ...c5.

pieces.why: Covers f5 and h7. With Qc2 it forms a battery against h7.
Pins the f6 knight; adds pressure on the e7 square and the e-file.
The open file. First rook there wins it.
Keeps c3 free for the pawn, then reroutes to g3 or e5 via f3.

key_squares.why: Outpost for your knight (Nf3-e5).
Whoever owns it can invade on e7/e8.
If Black plays ...c5 and ...cxd4, put a knight on d4 to blockade the isolated d5 pawn.

white.why: Attacks d5. Gives you an isolated d4 pawn but very active pieces; use only when your pieces are ready.
The quiet move: secures d4 and gives the queen c2.

black.why: Black's main active plan. After ...cxd4 Nxd4, Black has the isolated d5 pawn.
If Black plays ...c5-c4 hitting your Bd3, go Be2 and break with b3.

plans.title: Own the e-file
steps: Castle first.
Re1 before Black gets ...Re8.
Trade pieces that defend e7/e8 (Bg5xf6 or Bxe7).

plans.title: Pin and battery on h7
steps: Bg5 pins the f6 knight.
Nbd2, c3, Qc2: queen and bishop aim at h7.
Bxf6 at the right moment removes h7's defender.

plans.title: Blockade the isolated d5 pawn
steps: If Black plays ...c5 and ...cxd4, recapture Nxd4.
Knight on d4, rook on e1, then Nd2-f3/b3 and Be3.
Trade pieces: the isolated pawn gets weaker as pieces come off.

opponent_plans.title: ...Bg4 pin and ...Re8
steps: Black pins your f3 knight and fights for the e-file.

opponent_plans.title: ...c5 activity

Blockade d4 and simplify.

traps.title: The early pin backfires: ...Bg4 before castling
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 exd5 4. Bd3 Nf6 5. Nf3 Bd6 6. O-O Bg4 7. Re1+
traps.explanation: Black pinned your knight before castling. Re1+ checks along the open file: ...Be7 loses time and ...Kf8 loses castling. The open e-file punishes a king left in the middle.

traps.title: The knight on e7 stands on your file
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 exd5 4. Bd3 Bd6 5. Nf3 Ne7 6. O-O O-O 7. Re1 Bf5 8. Bg5
traps.explanation: Black's knight on e7 sits on the file you control. Bg5 attacks it, and Black has to spend time on defence while you finish developing.

if_deviates.why: Gain a tempo on the queen, as against the Scandinavian. You are clearly better.
Same set-up: c3 takes b4 and d4 is solid.
Black's pawn on c4 can be undermined by b3.
Take space. Black's e6 pawn and pieces get cramped (Benoni-like with an extra tempo).
Black gives you the full centre; just develop.
Develop with tempo on the queen; never move the king.

mistakes_to_avoid: Playing passively because the position looks drawish: develop fast and take the e-file first.
Allowing ...Re8 with check ideas while your king is still in the centre.
Recapturing ...cxd4 with the c-pawn when Nxd4 gives you a blockade square.
Putting the c1-bishop on d2: g5 or f4 is much more active.

quiz.question: Symmetric position, you move first. What is the most important file?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 exd5 4. Bd3 Nf6 5. Nf3 Bd6 6. O-O O-O
quiz.explanation: The e-file is the only open file. Get a rook there first.

quiz.question: Black took ...cxd4. How should you recapture?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 e6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 exd5 4. Bd3 c5 5. Nf3 Nc6 6. c3 Nf6 7. O-O cxd4

French Exchange: 4...c5, keep the c-file shut and blockade d5

wo-offbeat-first.title: Offbeat first moves (1...b6, 1...Nc6, 1...a6, 1...g5, 1...f5): centre, develop, castle
extra_anchors: 1. e4 Nc6 2. Nf3
wo-offbeat-first.summary: Against rare first moves you do not need theory. Black is giving you the centre: take it with d4, protect e4 with a piece (Bd3, Nc3, Qe2), develop toward the centre and castle. You score worst against 1...b6, mostly because e4 gets hit and pieces get lost to tricks, so learn the Owen set-up and its trap.

goals.white: e4 + d4, protect e4 with Bd3/Nc3/Qe2, develop Nf3 and castle; then gain more space (e5, c4) or attack.
goals.black: Hit your centre from the side (...Bb7 on e4, ...c5, ...Nc6 on d4) and get a playable but passive position.

structure.name: Free centre: e4 + d4 against a hypermodern set-up
structure.description: You own the centre; Black has fianchettoed bishops or knights aimed at it. Keep the centre protected and it will cramp Black for the whole game.

pieces.why: Protects e4 against ...Bb7 and aims at the kingside.
Second defender of e4, supports e5.
Normal development; keeps the 1...Nc6 2.Nf3 e5 Scotch transposition.

key_squares.why: Black's fianchettoed bishop and knights target it.
Push here to kick a knight from f6 and gain space.

Grab even more space against slow set-ups.

traps.pgn: 1. e4 g5 2. d4 Bg7 3. Bxg5

Pirc-like; develop with the big centre. Against ...Bg4, h3 or Be2.
Alekhine ideas with a free extra tempo for you.
A French where Black's knight blocks the c-pawn.
A move that doesn't fight for the centre; take it all.

Leaving e4 unprotected against a bishop on b7.
Chasing pawns or bishops with the queen instead of developing.

wo-petroff.title: Petroff (2...Nf6): 3.Nxe5, then 5.Nc3 and castle long
extra_anchors: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 d6 4. Nf3 Nxe4 5. Nc3
wo-petroff.summary: Black counter-attacks e4 instead of defending e5. Take on e5 first. If Black copies you too early with 3...Nxe4?, 4.Qe2! punishes it. After the correct 3...d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4, play 5.Nc3: swap knights, recapture dxc3 and castle long. Your pieces come out fast and you attack with h4/g4. Against the Stafford Gambit (3...Nc6) just take, play d3, Be2, c3 and avoid the traps.

goals.white: Win time with 5.Nc3 Nxc3 6.dxc3, develop Be3/Qd2/O-O-O, and storm the kingside with h4-h5 and g4.
goals.black: Equalise with symmetry and simple development; in the Stafford, set traps against f2 and your king.

structure.description: You have pawns on c2/c3 and no d- or e-pawn; Black has d6. The doubled pawns are not a weakness here: they protect your long-castled king and open the d-file for your rook.

traps.title: Copy-cat 3...Nxe4? 4.Qe2!
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 Nxe4 4. Qe2 Nf6 5. Nc6+
traps.explanation: The queen pins down the e-file. If the knight retreats, Nc6+ is a discovered check that wins the queen. After 4...Qe7 5.Qxe4 d6 6.d4 dxe5 7.dxe5 you keep a lasting edge.

traps.title: 5...Bf5?? 6.Qe2: the pinned knight
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 d6 4. Nf3 Nxe4 5. Nc3 Bf5 6. Qe2

traps.title: Stafford: don't play 6.Bg5??
traps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 Nc6 4. Nxc6 dxc6 5. d3 Bc5 6. Bg5 Nxe4 7. Bxd8 Bxf2+ 8. Ke2 Bg4#
traps.explanation: The famous Stafford mate. Grabbing the queen loses the king. 6.Be2 stops ...Bg4 checks and is safe.

Win the e4 pawn: the knight is pinned again.

Forgetting 4.Nf3 after 3...d6: the knight on e5 is attacked.

wo-philidor.title: Philidor (2...d6): 3.d4, the Scotch-player's answer
wo-philidor.summary: Black defends e5 with a pawn and shuts in his own f8-bishop. You hit the centre at once with 3.d4, just like in the Scotch. After ...exd4 you get a Scotch-type position with an extra pull (Black's d6 pawn is passive); against ...Bg4 you take on e5 and use the Opera-Game ideas; against the Lion (...Nf6, ...Nbd7) you develop Bc4, O-O, Re1 and keep the space.

goals.white: Open the centre with d4, develop fast (Nc3, Bc4 or Bf4, Qd2), and use your space or a pawn storm after opposite castling.
goals.black: Hold e5 with ...Nbd7/...Be7/...c6 (the Lion), or give up the centre with ...exd4 and play a solid cramped game.

structure.name: Scotch-like: e4 vs d6 (after ...exd4) / Lion: d4+e4 vs d6+e5
structure.description: After ...exd4 Nxd4 you have the e4 pawn against Black's d6: more space, a half-open d-file and a passive black position. In the Lion, the centre stays locked-ish with tension on d4/e5; your space and the f7 weakness decide.

After ...exd4, presses d6 and prepares O-O-O.
Qd2 for long castling; Qb3 hits f7 and b7 together.
e1 protects e4 in the Lion; d1 hits d6 after O-O-O.

Backward pawn on the half-open d-file after ...exd4.
Space-gaining push against ...Nc6 or ...c6.

Pawn storm after O-O-O in the ...exd4 line.

black.why: Gives up the centre for freedom.
Black's freeing break; often costs a pawn if prepared badly.

f3, g4, h4-h5: opposite-side pawn storm.

wo-pirc.title: Pirc and Modern (1...d6 / 1...g6): Be3, Qd2, Bh6, h4-h5
wo-pirc.anchor: 1. e4 d6 2. d4 Nf6 3. Nc3 g6 4. Be3
extra_anchors: 1. e4 g6 2. d4 Bg7 3. Nc3 d6 4. Be3
1. e4 d6 2. d4 g6 3. Nc3 Bg7 4. Be3
wo-pirc.summary: Black lets you build a big centre and fianchettoes the bishop on g7. You use one simple attacking set-up against both the Pirc and the Modern: Be3 and Qd2, Bh6 to trade the g7 bishop, then long castling or h4-h5 to open the h-file. It is the same plan Fischer used against Robatsch's Scandinavian with ...g6.

goals.white: Keep the e4+d4 centre, swap Black's dark bishop with Bh6, and attack the king with h4-h5.
goals.black: Strike the centre later with ...c5, ...e5 or ...c6 and ...b5, and use the g7 bishop against d4.

structure.name: Big centre e4+d4 vs fianchetto (Pirc/Modern)
structure.description: You have two centre pawns, Black has d6 and g6. If Black does nothing, you have more space everywhere. Black's counterplay comes from ...c5 or ...e5 breaks and queenside expansion with ...b5.

pieces.why: Trades the g7 bishop, Black's best defender.
Supports Bh6 and recaptures on h6, right next to Black's king.
Simple development; f3 also guards h4 and g5.
Long castling with an h-pawn storm is the most direct. If Black hits the queenside fast (...b5-b4), castle short.

key_squares.why: Your bishop and then queen land here.
Black's key bishop; once it is gone the dark squares near the king are weak.
e4-e5 kicks the f6 knight away from h7's defence.

white.why: Open the h-file toward the castled king.
Kick the f6 knight; with a queen on h6, Qxh7 mate patterns appear.
Gain space when Black plays ...c5 (keep the centre closed while you attack).

black.why: The best counter against Bh6/Qxh6: hit d4 at once.
Fight for the centre; dxe5 dxe5 and Qxd8 often leads to a pleasant endgame for you.
Kick the c3 knight away from e4.

plans.title: Swap the dragon bishop
steps: Be3 and Qd2.
Bh6 when Black has castled (or is about to).
After ...Bxh6 Qxh6 the queen sits next to the king.

plans.title: h-pawn storm
steps: O-O-O (or keep the king in the centre for a moment).
h4-h5, hxg6 to open the h-file.
Rook on h1 joins the attack.

plans.title: Centre clamp against ...c5
steps: Meet ...c5 with d5.
Black's g7 bishop (if still there) bites on granite.
Then continue with the kingside plan.

opponent_plans.title: Queenside counter-attack
steps: ...c6, ...b5, ...b4 to kick Nc3 and hit e4.
Answer with a3/a4 or castle short if the storm is too fast.

opponent_plans.title: Early ...Ng4 to grab the Be3
steps: Black hits the bishop before Qd2.
Bg5 keeps it; then h3 kicks the knight and Black has lost time.

traps.title: Early ...Ng4 just loses time
traps.pgn: 1. e4 d6 2. d4 Nf6 3. Nc3 g6 4. Be3 Ng4 5. Bg5 h6 6. Bh4 g5 7. Bg3
traps.explanation: Black chased your bishop but weakened the whole kingside and the g4 knight is loose. Be2 and h3 or h4 follow with a clear advantage.

traps.title: The open h-file (Fischer vs Robatsch)
traps.pgn: 1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Qxd5 3. Nc3 Qd8 4. d4 g6 5. Bf4 Bg7 6. Qd2 Nf6 7. O-O-O c6 8. Bh6 O-O 9. h4
traps.explanation: Same set-up against a fianchetto: Bh6 trades the g7 bishop and h4-h5 opens the h-file. Black was lost in 20 moves.

if_deviates.why: Same set-up; if ...b5, keep the knight on c3 with a3 or play Bd3.
Transposes to the Philidor Lion (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.Nc3). Play Bc4, O-O, Re1.
Transposes to your Philidor with 3.d4.
Gain space with d5, or take: 4.dxc5 Bxc3+ 5.bxc3 Qa5 6.Qd4 is good for you.
Black wants ...b5; keep it simple and develop.

mistakes_to_avoid: Pushing pawns (f4, g4) before developing: Black's breaks hit an unfinished centre.
Allowing ...Ng4 to swap your Be3: retreat to g5 or f4 and kick the knight with h3.
Castling long into a fast ...b5-b4 storm without counting moves.
Taking on h6 with the queen and then forgetting about ...c5 hitting d4: answer d5.

quiz.question: Black has castled behind the g7 bishop. What is the key attacking move?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 d6 2. d4 Nf6 3. Nc3 g6 4. Be3 Bg7 5. Qd2 O-O
quiz.explanation: Bh6 removes the best defender. After ...Bxh6 Qxh6 the queen is next to the king.

quiz.question: Black hits back with ...c5. Best answer?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 d6 2. d4 Nf6 3. Nc3 g6 4. Be3 Bg7 5. Qd2 O-O 6. Bh6 Bxh6 7. Qxh6 c5
quiz.explanation: d5 gains space and keeps lines shut in the middle while you attack on the kingside.

quiz.question: Which pawn opens lines against the castled king?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 g6 2. d4 Bg7 3. Nc3 d6 4. Be3 c6 5. Qd2 b5 6. Nf3 Nd7 7. Bd3 Ngf6 8. Bh6 Bxh6 9. Qxh6
quiz.explanation: h4-h5 and hxg6 opens the h-file for your rook and queen.

lines.name: Modern 1...g6: same set-up, Be3, Qd2, Bh6

wo-scandinavian.title: Scandinavian (1...d5): 3.Nc3 and develop around the queen
extra_anchors: 1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Nf6
wo-scandinavian.summary: Black brings the queen out early. Every developing move that also hits the queen is a free tempo. Your set-up is the same against every queen move: Nc3, Nf3, d4, a bishop to c4/d3/e2, castle, then use the lead in development.

goals.white: Develop fast with tempo on the queen, keep the d4 pawn, castle, and open lines (d5 or Ne5) while you are ahead in development.
goals.black: Get the queen to a safe square (a5, d8, d6), play ...c6, ...Bf5/...Bg4, ...e6 and reach a solid Caro-Kann-like position.

structure.name: d4 vs c6+e6 (Caro-like, half-open e-file for White)
structure.description: You have a pawn on d4, Black has pawns on c6 and e6 and no d-pawn. You have more space and the d4-d5 break. Black is solid but a little passive; the light bishop on f5/g4 is his best piece.

pieces.why: Hits the queen on move 3. Later it jumps to d5 (when Bd2 uncovers on a5) or e4.
Against ...Qa5, Bd2 breaks the pin on c3 and sets up Nd5/Nb5 discovered attacks on the queen.
Aims at f7 and e6. Against ...Qe5+/...Qe6+ it goes to e2 to block.
From e5 it hits f7/c6 and supports g4 to chase a bishop on f5/g6.
Black's best piece. Swap it with Bd3 or Nh4, or win the bishop pair with h3 when it goes to g4.

key_squares.why: Your knight jumps here with discovered attacks; the d4-d5 break opens lines.
Outpost for the f3 knight.
After ...Bxf3 Qxf3, your queen hits b7: ...Qxd4?? Qxb7 wins the rook.

white.why: Open the centre when you are ahead in development and the black king is still in the middle.

black.why: Hits d4. Answer by keeping the d-pawn defended or pushing d5.
Rare with the queen out; usually it just opens lines for you.

plans.title: Develop with tempo, then castle
steps: Nc3 hitting the queen.
Nf3, d4 and a bishop (c4 vs ...Qa5, e2 vs ...Qe5+/...Qe6+).
Castle, then Re1 or Qe2/O-O-O.

plans.title: The Bd2 + Nd5 trick
steps: Against ...Qa5 play Bd2: the bishop now faces the queen.
When the c6 pawn or the f6 knight is loose, Nd5 uncovers on a5.
If ...cxd5, Bxa5 wins the queen; otherwise Nxf6+ wrecks Black's kingside.

plans.title: Bishop pair after ...Bg4
steps: h3 asks the bishop.
After ...Bxf3 Qxf3 you have two bishops and pressure on b7.
Castle long, play d5 or Ne4 to open lines for the bishops.

opponent_plans.title: Solid ...c6, ...Bf5, ...e6, ...Nbd7
steps: Black builds a Caro-Kann shell and waits.
Your answer: Ne5 and g4 to chase the f5 bishop, or Bd2 and Nd5 tricks.

opponent_plans.title: ...Bg4 and ...Nc6 against d4
steps: Black piles up on d4.
Keep d4 protected (Be3, c3) and use h3 to kick the bishop.

traps.title: Bd2 and Nd5: the queen is lost
traps.pgn: 1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Qxd5 3. Nc3 Qa5 4. Nf3 Nf6 5. d4 c6 6. Bc4 Bf5 7. Bd2 e6 8. Nd5 cxd5 9. Bxa5
traps.explanation: With the bishop on d2 facing the queen, the knight jump to d5 is a discovered attack. Taking the knight loses the queen.

traps.title: ...Qxd4?? Qxb7
traps.pgn: 1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Qxd5 3. Nc3 Qd8 4. d4 Nf6 5. Nf3 Bg4 6. h3 Bxf3 7. Qxf3 Qxd4 8. Qxb7
traps.explanation: After Black gives up his light bishop, b7 is undefended. Grabbing d4 loses the rook in the corner.

traps.title: The pinned bishop: ...Bg4 after Be2
traps.pgn: 1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Qxd5 3. Nc3 Qe5+ 4. Be2 Bg4 5. d4 Qd6 6. Bxg4
traps.explanation: Your Be2 was pinned by the queen on e5, so ...Bg4 looked safe. d4 kicks the queen off the e-file, and now the bishop is free to take on g4.

if_deviates.why: The queen on d6 can be hit by Nb5 or Bf4. Same development as always.
Usually transposes to the main line after ...Nf6 and ...Bf5. Against ...Bg4, h3.
Pin the knight and castle; Black's queen and knight are clumsy.
The Portuguese gambit. Keep the pawn with simple development; 4.f3 is sharper.
Build the c4+d4 centre and develop.

mistakes_to_avoid: Playing 2.Nf3 or 2.e5 instead of taking on d5: you score far worse with them.
Blocking ...Qe5+ or ...Qe6+ with the queen: keep the queen and the e-file for later.
Chasing the queen with pawns (b4, a3) instead of developing pieces.
Forgetting that Bd2 is needed against ...Qa5: without it, Nc3 is pinned and ...Bb4 hurts.

quiz.question: Black has played 3...Qa5. What is White's set-up?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Qxd5 3. Nc3 Qa5
quiz.explanation: Develop. The queen will be hit later by Bd2 + Nd5/Nb5 tricks, not by pawn moves.

quiz.question: White to move. Which move uses the Bd2 battery?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Qxd5 3. Nc3 Qa5 4. Nf3 Nf6 5. d4 c6 6. Bc4 Bf5 7. Bd2 e6
quiz.explanation: 8.Nd5 uncovers the bishop on the queen; 8...cxd5?? 9.Bxa5, and after 8...Qd8 9.Nxf6+ you remove Black's best defender.

quiz.question: Black would like to grab 7...Qxd4. Why is that a blunder?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Qxd5 3. Nc3 Qd8 4. d4 Nf6 5. Nf3 Bg4 6. h3 Bxf3 7. Qxf3
choices: 8.Qxb7 hits the rook on a8 and wins material
It isn't: d4 is a free pawn
quiz.explanation: Black's light bishop is gone, so b7 has no defender. After 7...Qxd4 8.Qxb7 the a8 rook falls. Black usually plays 7...c6 first; then you guard d4 with Be3.

quiz.question: 3...Qe5+. How do you block?
quiz.pgn: 1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Qxd5 3. Nc3 Qe5+
choices: 4.Be2, then d4 and Nf3 with tempo
quiz.explanation: Block with a developing piece. Then d4 or Nf3 gains time on the queen.

Scandinavian 3...Qa5 4.Nf3 Bg4: take the bishop pair
Scandinavian 3...Qd8: d4, Nf3, bishop pair after ...Bg4

headers.Theme: Panov: blockade d5, trade pieces, attack the weak pawns, win with the good bishop

Watch Karpov: he blockades d5 with a knight, trades every piece he can, and only then attacks White's weak pawns. When the queens come off, the endgame is his.

headers.Theme: Exchange Caro-Kann: the minority attack ...b5-b4 beats White's kingside storm

caro-dzindzichashvili-karpov-1988.intro: The Exchange Variation in its purest form. Watch three things: Karpov develops the light bishop to g4 BEFORE playing ...e6, he answers Qb3 calmly, and then he pushes his queenside pawns (...b5, ...a5, ...b4, ...a4) at White's c3 pawn. That pawn march is the minority attack, and it is Black's main plan in this structure.

headers.Theme: Two Knights 3...Bg4: give up the bishop for the f3 knight, take central space, and win the race on the queenside

Black's answer is simple: pin and take the f3 knight with the bishop, then grab the centre with pawns. White keeps the e5 wedge with Qe2, c4, b3 and f4, puts the bishop on a3, and then cashes in with a burst of tactics (c5 and e6) that leaves Black's position in pieces. Then a clean technical finish with passed pawns.

st-botvinnik-vidmar-1936.intro: The textbook IQP attack. White gets an isolated pawn on d4, and in return free lines and the e5 square. Watch three things: the knight jumps to e5, the queen and bishops aim at Black's king, and the f-pawn joins in. Black never blockades d5 firmly and never trades enough pieces. Notes are based on Alekhine's annotations, rewritten for the structure.

st-nimzowitsch-salwe-1911.intro: The most famous game about the advance pawn chain (French Advance, the same chain you get in the Caro-Kann Advance). Black does everything by the book: ...c5 hits the base, ...Nc6 and ...Qb6 pile on d4, ...f6 hits the head. Nimzowitsch answers with a surprise: he gives up the base and **blockades** the squares in front of Black's pawns with pieces. Black ends up with a backward e6 pawn that never moves freely. Notes follow Nimzowitsch's own ideas.

e4.why: White grabs the centre and opens lines for the queen and bishop.

d4.why: White takes the centre and frees the c1-bishop.

c4.why: The English. White fights for d5 from the side.

Nf3.why: Flexible. White waits to see your setup.

b3.why: Larsen's Opening. The bishop aims at your kingside from b2.

f4.why: The Bird. White controls e5 like a reversed Dutch.

g4.why: The Grob. Weakens White's kingside for good.

Nc3.why: The Van Geet. Often goes e4.

c6.why: The Caro-Kann: prepare ...d5 so that if White ever takes on d5, a PAWN recaptures.

d4.why: White builds the ideal pawn centre.

Nf3.why: White develops first and keeps options open. At club level this often leads to the Exchange.

Nc3.why: White develops and supports e4.

c4.why: The Accelerated Panov: White hits d5 before playing d4.

Bc4.why: A common club move aiming at f7.

d3.why: A quiet King's Indian Attack setup: d3, Nd2, Ngf3, g3, Bg2, O-O.

f4.why: White wants a kingside attack with f4-f5 one day.

Qf3.why: An early queen move. It blocks the f3 knight and can be chased.

d5.why: Strike at e4 at once. White must now trade, defend or push.

exd5.why: The Exchange Variation: White releases the tension and hopes for quiet, quick development.

e5.why: The Advance: White grabs space and takes the f6 square from your knight.

Nc3.why: White defends e4 with a knight.

f3.why: The Fantasy Variation: White protects e4 with a pawn.

cxd5.why: Recapture with the c-pawn. You keep a pawn in the centre and get the half-open c-file.

Bd3.why: The bishop aims at h7 and controls f5, so ...Bf5 is not possible right now.

Bb5+.why: A check that only offers a trade.

c4.why: The Panov-Botvinnik Attack. White attacks d5 again and will often end up with an isolated d4 pawn (IQP).

Nc6.why: Develop and hit d4 at once. The knight also supports a later ...b5.

c3.why: White protects d4 with a pawn. This is the Carlsbad structure with colours reversed.

Nf6.why: Guard d5 and h7, the two targets of White's Bd3.

Bf4.why: White develops the dark bishop outside the pawn chain before playing Nf3.

Nf3.why: The most natural move: White develops the knight first.

Bg4.why: The Caro-Kann rule: the light bishop comes OUT before ...e6. From g4 it hits the queen and will pin a knight on f3.

Qb3.why: White's standard trick: with the bishop gone from c8, b7 is attacked (and d5 too).

Qc8.why: Calmly guard b7 (Karpov's choice). The queen also keeps an eye on the c-file and f5.

Nd2.why: Development: the knight heads for f3 next to the other one, or supports e4.

e6.why: Now that the bishop is out, ...e6 makes d5 rock-solid and opens the f8 bishop.

Ngf3.why: White finishes development; the knight is pinned by your bishop.

Be7.why: Safe and solid: the bishop guards the king and f6. ...Bd6 is also fine.

O-O.why: Castle. Development is done; now the plan is the minority attack: ...Rb8 (or ...Qc7/...Rc8), ...b5, ...b4.

Rae1.why: White eyes e5 and the kingside.

Bh5.why: Keep the pin and prepare ...Bg6 to trade White's best attacking piece, the d3 bishop.

Bg4.why: Bishop out with a pin on the f3 knight, which defends d4.

e6.why: Now ...e6: the c8 bishop is already outside.

Bf4.why: White's bishop takes the b8-h2 diagonal.

Bd6.why: Challenge it. Trading dark bishops removes a piece that would support Ne5.

Qxd6.why: The queen recaptures and controls e5 and the b8-h2 diagonal.

Nbd2.why: White develops the last minor piece.

O-O.why: Castle. Now start the queenside plan.

Re1.why: White's rook takes the half-open e-file.

Rab8.why: The rook supports ...b5-b4: the minority attack. Your two queenside pawns will attack White's three.

e5.why: Advance with the knight already on f3.

d4.why: Now we have the Exchange Variation with Nf3 already played.

Bb5+.why: The same check with the knight already on f3.

Nc6.why: Same recipe: knight to c6 hitting d4, then ...Bg4 and ...Nf6.

Bd3.why: White puts the bishop on its best square.

Nc3.why: White develops and adds pressure on d5.

c3.why: Protects d4. This position is the same as 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.c3 Nf6 6.Nf3.

Bg4.why: Bishop out with a counter-pin. Both sides pin a knight.

h3.why: White asks the bishop to decide.

Bxf3.why: Take the knight. White's queen recaptures, but d4 loses a defender.

e6.why: Solid: d5 is protected, and the f8 bishop can develop.

Nf6.why: Develop and defend. Next ...Be7 and ...O-O, then use the c-file. If White takes on c6, ...bxc6 gives you more central pawns.

Bg4.why: Pin the f3 knight, which defends d4. Now d4 is a real target.

e6.why: Solid centre. If White ever plays h3, take on f3 and keep pressing d4.

Bd6.why: Active bishop aiming at h2. Next ...Nge7 or ...Nf6 and castle.

e6.why: Now ...e6.

Qxd6.why: Queen to d6 controls e5. Castle next, then ...Rab8 and ...b5.

Bd3.why: Develop and guard e4. Next O-O, then f4 and e5. If 7...Qh4, castle: 8.O-O covers f2.

Nc3.why: Simple development. If 5...Nxd4 6.Qxd4, your queen is great again.

Ng6.why: The knight goes to g6 to cover e5 and f4.

Be3.why: Develop. Next Qd2 and O-O-O, then f4 or h4-h5 to hit the g6 knight.

Qd2.why: Defend c3 and connect the rooks. Castle long next.

d5.why: Gain space with tempo: the knight must move, and every square is worse than c6.

Nce7.why: The common retreat. The knight blocks the f8-bishop.

c4.why: Grab more space. Your plan: Nc3, Be2 or Bd3, castle short, then c5 to open the queenside.

f5.why: Black's only active idea: hit back on the kingside with ...f5.

Nc3.why: Develop and add a guard to e4. If Black takes on e4, recapture with the knight onto a beautiful central square.

dxe5.why: Take the pawn and kick the knight.

Qe2.why: Attack the knight. It cannot stay: it must retreat or be swapped.

Nc3.why: Develop. Next Be3 or Bg5, O-O-O, and the e5 pawn cramps Black.

dxe5.why: Open the position against the weakened king. If 4...Nxe5 5.Nxe5 fxe5?? 6.Qh5+ wins: 6...g6 7.Qxe5+ forks king and rook, and 6...Ke7 7.Qxe5+ Kf7 8.Bc4+ is a crushing attack.

fxe5.why: Black keeps a pawn in the centre.

Bc4.why: Aim at g8 and f7. Black's king can no longer castle easily.

Ng5.why: Hit f7 twice. Black must find ...d5, and after 7.exd5 Black is just worse with a loose king.

Nxe5.why: Take the free pawn on e5. The knight is very strong here.

dxe4.why: Black takes back a centre pawn.

Bb5.why: Pin the c6 knight and pile up on it.

Bxc6.why: Give the bishop for the knight to ruin Black's pawns.
Black takes back with the bishop.

O-O.why: Castle. Next Nc3 and Re1 to win the loose e4 pawn.

Qxd4.why: Take back with the queen. This is exactly the 4...Nxd4 5.Qxd4 position by a different move order: same plan, Nc3, Bf4, O-O-O.

dxe5.why: Swap so the bishop has to recapture.

Bxe5.why: Black's bishop is in the centre.

f4.why: Kick the bishop with tempo. If 6...Qh4+ 7.g3, the check is over, the e5 bishop is still attacked, and Black loses material.

c3.why: Block with a pawn and attack the bishop. Note: if 4...exd4, the c3 pawn is pinned, but it can still capture the pinning bishop: 5.cxb4 wins a piece for two pawns.

Ba5.why: The bishop stays on the diagonal.

Nxe5.why: e5 is now undefended. White is a clean pawn up.
Take the pawn on e5. The e8-h5 diagonal is open.

Nxc6.why: Remove the defender and damage the pawns.

Qh5+.why: Check on the weak diagonal. If 6...g6, 7.Qe5+ wins the h8 rook.

Bg5+.why: Another check: Black must block with the knight.

Nc3.why: Bring the last minor piece in. Black's king is stuck in the centre, and e4 will fall.
Develop. Next Bg5 with tempo on the queen (or Be3), then Qd2 and O-O-O. Black's pieces are tangled.
